en: Now, the subject matter of the second chapter. Homage to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
Composed by the venerable Śivānubhava Śivācārya, the disciple of the illustrious Bhagavatpāda.
The Mirror of the Non-duality of Śiva. [Now begins the first chapter. Om, salutation to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. For the sake of the accomplishment of the aims of the worlds.
To the mouse-eared one (the rat-faced Gaṇeśa)—an alternative reading is *vṛṣaketave* (the bull-bannered Śiva)—who is the bridge for crossing the ocean of obstacles. || 1 ||
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
To the one who is the seed of the thirty-six principles, to the Supreme Self accompanied by Ambā. || 2 ||

I bow to the five teachers, the gurus of the world, who emerged from the mouths of the Five-Faced One (Śiva), who are incomparable through the five-syllable mantra, and who are the authors of the five aphorisms. (This verse is printed as an addition.)
To Vedavyāsa, the author of the Sūtras; and to Caitanya, the author of the Commentary (Vṛtti).
I take refuge in the venerable Nīlakaṇṭha, the author of the commentary, for the attainment of my desired goal. || 4 ||
To the teacher of all worlds, the physician for those afflicted by the disease of existence.
Salutation to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the treasury of all sciences. || 5 ||
[This is] the tradition descended through the lineage of the venerable Guru Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
I bow to the primordial creeper, the perfected consciousness, who is the very embodiment of Caitanya.
Born from the lotus-hand of him [the Lord], the crest-jewel of the Śiva-ācāryas.
I pay homage to the teacher of the Vaiśeṣika, the lord of ascetics Śivāditya.
Born from his lotus-hand, it is the moon of the six philosophical systems.
I bow to that supreme teacher, Viśveśvaraśivācārya.
From his glorious lotus-like hand, a yogi with matted hair was born.
I bow to the world-teacher, Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya. || 9 ||
He who is the manifestation of a non-inferior incarnation of Śambhu and the establisher of the Śaiva Āgamas.
He who indeed proclaimed the excellent commentary on the first [section] of the four Vedas.
May that illustrious Sadguru Nīlakaṇṭha Yatirāja, the mover of the world, who produced the nectar of the Bhāṣya in the ocean of the web of Vyāsa’s Sūtras, be victorious. 10.
Having churned the ocean of the *Nigama* with the mountain of his own scholarship, he distributed the nectar known as the *Bhāṣya*.
Victorious is that Lord Nīlakaṇṭha, the sovereign of ascetics, who is dense with virtues and who brought relief to living beings terrified by the poison of worldly existence. 11.
A peacock to the cobras of wicked disputants, he has gratified Śiva through his ascetic practices.
May that Nīlakaṇṭha himself, who has placed the lion’s roar upon the arguments of the scriptures, be victorious on this earth.
Indeed, Nīlakaṇṭha is an ocean of compassion, desiring to lift up those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence.
He descended to the earth specifically to compose this boat of a commentary marked with his own name. || 13 ||
To that Lord of the lion-throne of the Śiva-advaita philosophy established by him.
I bow to the venerable Śrīcidghana-guru, who is the very embodiment of pure consciousness. || 14 ||
He is the sun for the lotus-heart of those who have taken refuge in him;
he is the axe for splitting asunder the poisonous form of defilement.
Victorious is that supreme teacher of the gods, the embodiment of consciousness, who holds within his hand the realization of the true nature of his own self. 15.
By that one born from the lotus of his hand, a yogi through the experience of Śiva.
This treatise, titled *Śivādvaitadarpaṇa* (The Mirror of the Non-duality of Śiva), is now being composed. || 16 ||

Then the Blessed One Bādarāyaṇa, supremely compassionate and desiring to deliver people tormented by the heat of saṃsāra, knowing [the truth], attained the auspicious peace that is ultimate (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.14; Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1): "The knower of Brahman attains [Brahman]."
In accordance with such scriptural passages as: "Brahman is the supreme, the knower of truth, and infinite" (Kaivalya Upaniṣad 1.9);
"Having known Him, one transcends death; there is no other path for liberation" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8);
and "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; no other path exists for the journey" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12.7).

In order to bring about the knowledge of Brahman, which is the sole means for their liberation, he composed the *Śārīraka-sūtras*, the essence of the Upaniṣads; therein, at the very beginning, he enunciated the inquiry into Brahman with the aphorism: "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (*Brahma-sūtra* 1.1.1). Now, therefore...

In the phrase *brahmajijñāsā*, when the word *atha* (then) is intended to signify immediate succession (*ānantarya*), the inquiry arises as to what that succession is. Having stated that it is the succession to *dharma* (religious duty), when the further doubt arises as to what kind of *dharma* it is, [the text] distinguishes *dharma* by way of the categories of *paśudharma* (the duties of animals) and *patidharma* (the duties of masters).

With the intention that the first type of *paśu-dharma* (the duty of the bound soul) serves as a means to the knowledge of Brahman through a lineage by way of bestowing the *pati-dharma* (the duty of the Lord), whereas *pati-dharma* itself is a direct means to that [knowledge], he says: "In this context, the meaning of the word *atha*. [This concludes] the eight coverings (*aṣṭāvaraṇāni*).

The limbs of the devotee consist of the Śrī Guru, the Liṅga, the Jaṅgama, the water from the feet (pādodaka), the prasāda, the vibhūti, the rudrākṣa, and the mantra. Furthermore, the fivefold conduct (pañcācāra)—consisting of liṅgācāra, bhṛtyācāra, sadācāra, śivācāra, and gaṇācāra—are the duties of the devotee. As for their specific distinction:
Thus, by virtue of the relationship of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*),

the meaning is that since the five conducts (*pañcācāra*) qualified by the eight enclosures (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*) constitute the duty of the Lord (*pati-dharma*), one must desire to know Brahman immediately after attaining those [conducts]. And so it is stated in the *Kriyāsāra*:

Therefore, the non-interruption of *dharma* alone must be proclaimed; for *dharma* is considered to be twofold: the *paśudharma* (the duty of the beast) is the first, and the *patidharma* (the duty of the husband/master) is the second. One who practices the duties of the beast is not worthy of the duties of the master, just as an ant, having smelled the root of a tree, ascends it and obtains its fruit.

"Likewise, one who is solely intent on the duty toward the husband— just as a bird that has come to a fruit-bearing tree obtains the fruit upon seeing it, so too does he quickly deserve that [result]. Herein,
the meaning of the word *atha* (now/then) refers to the eight enclosures (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*).
The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) expresses the immediate sequence following the attainment of the duties of a husband in the form of the distinguished fivefold conduct (*pañcācāra*).
Indeed, this word denotes the completion of the qualifications (*adhikāra*). And so it is said in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (6.22–23):
"This supreme secret of the Vedānta, which was imparted in a former age, must not be given to one who is not tranquil."

Nor, again, to one who is not a son or a disciple. For that high-souled one who possesses supreme devotion to the Divine, and as toward the Divine so toward the Guru—for him these meanings declared here truly shine forth. [This is to be taught] to one who has studied the Vedas, whose senses are conquered, and who follows the established eight-fold enclosure (aṣṭāvaraṇa) at all times.

"This non-dual Śiva-advaita should be given to one who is endowed with good conduct, possessed of wisdom, and desirous of liberation"—such is the statement of the Śruti and Āgama. Since the attainment of the husband’s dharma (patidharma) is the very fulfillment of qualification (*adhikāra-pūrṇatva*), for that reason, the inquiry into Brahman (*brahma-jijñāsā*) must be undertaken; this is the sense.

The author's intention is that, in order to avoid the charge of mere restatement (anuvāda) regarding the term *jijñāsā* in the aphorism "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*),
and to ensure the engagement of persons in the scripture, the word "should be performed" (*kartavyā*) must be supplied,
and the term *jijñāsā* must be taken as indicating (lakṣaṇā) "investigation" (*vicāra*). Now, here...

If it is argued that it is improper to apply figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to the word *jijñāsā*—which consists of both a base (*prakṛti*) and a suffix (*pratyaya*)—because it is a sentence, since a sentence lacks a primary denotative power (*śakya*), and consequently lacks even figurative indication, which is defined as a relationship with the primary denotation; we reply: no. By means of the suffix, through non-abandoning figurative indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*), "inquiry" (*vicāra*) is conveyed, and by the base...
Since the knowledge of the object to be proven (*sādhya*) is expressed through non-abandoning indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*), it must be accepted that there are indeed two types of indication.

On this point, some maintain that there is only a single indication residing in the entire collection of base and suffix; and they argue that there is no absence of a relationship between the primary meaning (*śakya*), because the relationship exists precisely through the members of that collection.

They say that this is because the relationship with the capacity of the aggregate is also possible; however, that is not correct, because since the words, their meanings, and their relationships—which are characterized by distributive occurrence (*vyāsajyavṛtti*)—are multiple, it is impossible for the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to be unitary. And thus, where...
When another entity is indicated by words through their connection with the sentence-meaning, that indication (lakṣaṇā) resides in the sentence itself;
for example, in "Eat [this as] poison" (*viṣaṃ bhuṅkṣva*) and so forth. In the technical treatises, this is conventionally termed "word-indication" (*padalakṣaṇā*), as it is distinct from the former.
This being the case, even in the present context, there is not a single indication belonging to the whole, nor to the individual members of that whole.

Because the relation is distinct due to the distinction [of the relata]; nor is it a desired consequence that the definitions are one simply because they produce a single cognition. For if that were the case, since the object of investigation would be established by just one of the two definitions, there would be no need for both definitions.

Because the acceptance of that [meaning] as being present [in the base] would result in redundancy, one must therefore accept two instances of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since both the base and the suffix function as indicators; for the resulting complexity (*gaurava*) is of no consequence here. In this context, regarding the statement "an inquiry (*vicāra*) must be performed for the sake of knowledge," knowledge is aimed at as the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and the inquiry is the means (*sādhana*).
It is enjoined; for inquiry is connected as a means toward the knowledge that constitutes the meaning of the root [of the verb].
Therefore, because it serves as a definition, the treatise consisting of the inquiry into Brahman must be commenced—this is the intended meaning of the aphorism that inaugurates the treatise. || 1 ||
Now, if it is asked what Brahman is and what its characteristic is, it is said in reply:
Brahman is indeed Paraśiva, who consists of the six planes (ṣaṭsthala) and is denoted by the synonym *ghanaliṅga*.
Its characteristic, however, is that Brahman is qualified by the subtle power (*śakti*) whose nature is both conscious (*cit*) and unconscious (*acit*).

The term "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the individual soul (*jīvātman*). Subtlety consists in being pure by nature; therefore, even though the liberated soul (*muktātman*) is characterized by a power that is both conscious and unconscious and is pure by nature, there is no over-extension to it, because that [liberated] power lacks natural purity. Nor [does this definition apply to] the one whose birth and so forth...

It must be said that there is no contradiction with the definition in the Sūtra, because the Sūtra establishes as the defining characteristic the state of being the cause of the world's birth and so forth; for when that is established as the definition,
even the causality of each individual act— birth, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace— is unique to [Brahman] alone and does not belong to anything else.
Since it is necessary to intend five distinct characteristics that are mutually independent, one should—
out of a desire for brevity rather than prolixity—
intend a single, inclusive characteristic by means of a causal relationship (*hetu-hetumad-bhāva*) common to both the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*).
Because, at this moment, the definition of the Knowable Brahman— which has become the object of inquiry— is untenable; therefore,
since it is necessary first to intend to state the essential definition (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) of the Knowable Brahman,
and because the status of being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world is impossible without such a power, [the following is stated] first.

For it is appropriate to state only that which constitutes His essential definition, namely, the characteristic of being qualified by the subtle powers of both consciousness (cit) and non-consciousness (acid). || 2 ||

If it is objected: "Let the very nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānandatva) be the definition of its essential form; what is the use of this future definition?", we say no. For, by intending to express the relationship of attribute and substratum between power and the possessor of power, the definition is established precisely by accepting that the attributes of Brahman—Being, Consciousness, and Bliss—are of the nature of a single, underlying power.

In the commentary on the *Ānandamaya-Adhikaraṇa* as well, it is stated that the nature of the Supreme Power, which is the supreme ether resting upon the Supreme Brahman, is the attribute of the Supreme Brahman known as Ānandamaya, whose form is abundant bliss (*pracurānanda*).
(The meaning is: "Because it has been accepted by the venerable Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya.
This is the relevant passage from his commentary: *taddhetuvyapadeśācca* [Brahma-sūtra 1.1.15]:
"For who indeed could breathe, who could live, if this bliss did not exist in this space?")
For it is he alone who causes bliss;

because he is designated as the cause of bliss by virtue of bestowing bliss upon all living beings, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is indeed Paraśiva himself. For he who is himself characterized by abundant bliss causes others to be blissful, just as...

One who is distinguished by abundant knowledge makes others possessed of knowledge; therefore, Paraśiva alone is "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya). When it is said that Paraśiva, distinguished by abundant bliss, is "consisting of bliss," [it follows that] he is indeed other than [anyone else].

It is understood that [the Self] consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), because it is understood as having Brahman as its tail and support (*brahmapucchaṃ pratiṣṭhā*) by virtue of being the substratum of Brahman. Therefore, having raised the objection that the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is the one consisting of bliss, [the Sūtrakāra] says: "And it is proclaimed as being exactly that which is described in the mantra" (Sūtra 1.1.16). For this reason also, [the Self] is distinguished by the power of the consciousness-ether (*cidambaraśakti*).

Paraśiva alone is the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). In the mantra, "He who knows Him hidden in the secret cave, in the highest ether," the subject under discussion is the "inner Self" (*antarātman*); and in the Brāhmaṇa, He is celebrated as *ānandamaya* because He is characterized by an abundance of bliss.

This is because the mantra and the brāhmaṇa have a single meaning; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of abandoning the subject under discussion and introducing something not under discussion. Furthermore, since the state of being "within" is asserted, and no other thing within is taught, that which is indicated as the supreme Brahman to be attained by the mantra, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," [is the same].

"One approaches that very Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*)"—thus, in the Brāhmaṇa, it is described as "consisting of bliss" because it is characterized by abundant bliss. Since no other goal to be attained is heard [in the text], otherwise there would follow the abandonment of what is stated in scripture and the assumption of what is not stated. Therefore:

The Self, whose nature is the supreme ether and who consists of bliss, is so heard in scripture. There is no cause superior to the universe, namely the Supreme Brahman, which is called "Brahman, which is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite.
From this very Self, indeed, the ether was produced.
Thus, the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), which is heard in scripture as the material cause of the manifold universe beginning with space, is the supreme ether (paramākāśa).
That its nature is that of the supreme ether is understood from the statement: "If this space were not bliss. Furthermore, "Brahman is the tail, the support" refers to Brahman.

It is understood as the substratum of the supreme ether, whose nature is abundant bliss; for this very reason, it is understood as being supported by Brahman through the statement, "That is one [unit] of Brahman’s bliss. Furthermore, by such passages as, "He understood that bliss is indeed Brahman," and "From bliss alone, indeed, these beings are born," it is established.

It is designated as the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of all beings. In that regard, the designation of bliss as Brahman—namely, "Bliss is Brahman"—is due to its non-difference from Brahman by virtue of being an attribute of Brahman. This very knowledge of Bhārgava and Vāruṇi is established in the supreme firmament; [it is established] in that which is the essential nature of the attributes of Brahman, whose form is supreme bliss.

In the supreme void (*paramavyoman*), which is the self of consciousness (*cidātman*), the synonym for the supreme power (*paramaśakti*)— namely, the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*)— the Vāruṇī-vidyā is said to be complete. Thereafter, that supreme power, whose form is the supreme ether (*paramākāśa*), which is the very essence of the nature of Brahman and consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), is so called because it is characterized by that [consciousness] as its substrate (*dharmin*).
The term "Pratiṣṭhā" (the Foundation) refers to the Supreme Brahman, and the individual soul (*jīva*), consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), is its worshiper.

Because no distinction is perceived between the foundational substratum— the Supreme Śiva, who is Brahman— and the blissful one (*ānandamaya*) who constitutes His attribute and is of the nature of Śakti, it is generally understood that "the Self consisting of bliss is Brahman."

This has been aphorized by the author of the Sūtras in the statement, "The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of repetition. This is because it has been accepted by the venerable Bhagavatpāda himself.
Furthermore, there is no possibility of the two contradictory powers—consisting of the sentient and the insentient—which enter into the definition you have stated, existing in one and the same place.

Since, even in your own view, there must necessarily be the complexity (gaurava) arising from the desire to state the individual definitions of "being qualified by the subtle power of the nature of consciousness" and "being qualified by the subtle power of the nature of non-consciousness" as mutually independent, the definition found in the Sūtra alone is correct.

It should be stated that it is appropriate to say so; for in our view, we accept that the power which is of the nature of an attribute of Brahman is of the nature of *cicchakti* (conscious power), while that which is of the nature of its reflection is of the nature of *acitchakti* (unconscious power). Thus, [regarding] *cicchakti*...

Since there is no contradiction in the reflection and the power of consciousness both being attributes of Brahman, the intention is to indicate that the one [Brahman] alone is qualified by a subtle power consisting of both consciousness and non-consciousness, by combining these two powers through a cumulative conjunction (*samuccaya*). || 3 ||

If it be asked, "How is the establishment of Brahman as the regulator of the birth, sustenance, and dissolution of the world possible if you accept the definition stated by you?"— listen: just as the mass of foam and bubbles produced upon the waves of the ocean is of the very same nature as that ocean itself.
Likewise, within the Supreme Brahman characterized by power (*śakti*), the origination and so forth of the world are seen to be of that very same nature;
nothing whatsoever is perceived apart from it. Thus, it is stated by the Lord in the *Atharvaśiras* (in the first section): "I alone existed in the beginning."

"I exist and I shall exist; there is nothing whatsoever other than myself. Thus, by the statement "I am Brahman" and so forth, the universal form of the Self has been elaborated. Regarding that universal form, the very reason stated is its entry, in the words: "He entered into the interior of the interior. Therefore...
Because it follows by implication that Brahman is the controller of the birth and other states of the world, which is not established as separate from Himself.

Furthermore, [the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8 states]: "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold; knowledge, strength, and action are His inherent nature. And [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.2 states]: "Rudra is indeed one; there is no second."

The Śruti passages beginning with "He who dwells in these worlds, ruling them by his supreme powers" (tasthe ya imān lokānīśata īśanībhiḥ) and others likewise declare that the Supreme Brahman, Paraśiva, who consists of the six abodes (ṣaṭsthala), is characterized by innate and infinite powers of creating, governing, and protecting the universe.
They say:

in short, the essential nature of the Great Consciousness and Bliss is the form of the Great Sovereignty that bestows all sentient and insentient things; it is innate and devoid of limitations such as space and time.

The Supreme Power (paramaśakti) is said to be the unique attribute of the Supreme Śiva (paraśiva), which constitutes his very nature. Apart from that [Power], the Supreme Śiva’s omniscience, omnipotence, causality of all things,
sovereignty over all, being the object of worship for all, his role as the benefactor of all, his status as the cause of all human goals, and so forth— [all these would be impossible].

This is not possible. Therefore, it should be understood that there is no inconsistency whatsoever in that [Brahman], characterized by inconceivable power, being the regulator of the birth and so forth of the world. || 4 ||

Is it not said [in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5]: "The one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form"? And [in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10]: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti, but the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā. Thus, there is the quality of being the progenitor of many offspring.

And its nature as the *parā-prakṛti* denoted by the term *māyā* follows from the scriptural account of that [prakṛti] as having the form of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, inferred from its red and other colors; furthermore, since it is observed that the insentience (*jāḍya*) inherent in that [prakṛti] persists in jars and other objects, [the principle] is "Being alone" (*sad eva*) in accordance with that [insentience]. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1)

Since she alone is easily understood as that which is denoted by the word "Being" (sat) heard in causal passages such as "In the beginning, this was Being," it follows that Śakti alone is perceived as the material cause of the universe.
If it is asked, "How then is Brahman the material cause? it is replied as follows:

Both Brahman and Śakti are the material cause (*upādāna*), since the status of being a material cause heard in the supreme causal statements is applicable to both; and because it is logically consistent that both the properties of existence (*sattā*) and insentience (*jaḍya*) follow [the effect], as in "the pot exists" and "the pot is insentient. In that regard, Brahman is the material cause by virtue of its sovereignty.
The only distinction, however, is that Śakti exists through dependence [on another].
That which does not depend on anything else is the "unsupported" (anāśrita) Supreme Brahman; that which has this as its limit (antaḥ = avasānam) is "ending with the unsupported" (anāśritāntam).

The author’s intention is that the network of thirty-six principles, beginning with Śakti and ending with Earth, functions as dependent (paratantra). Here, this must be understood: that which begins with Śakti and ends with Anāśrita functions dependently; for whatever ends with Anāśrita functions dependently, just like a jar.

Objection: Let it be that principles (tattvas) other than Śakti exist in dependence upon her; however, Śakti herself does not [depend on anything], because she is the material cause of everything and thus the substratum of all principles. Reply: This is not so. Śakti must reside somewhere, because she is a property (dharma). Whatever is a property resides somewhere, just as the property "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) resides in a pot.

Thus, by means of inference, it is established that power (*śakti*) is dependent on something in some locus. Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of essential proof (*svarūpāsiddhi*) because power lacks the status of being a property (*dharma*); for [the following inference holds]: "Power is of the nature of a property, because it possesses occurrence (*vṛttimat*), like potness. By this inference, [its status as a property is established].

Because power (*śakti*) is of the nature of an attribute (*dharma*), there is no lack of proof regarding its own nature (*svarūpa*). Nor should it be argued that "power does not exist at all; how then can its being dependent [on a substratum] and so forth be inferred? For it would be improper to say that power does not exist, given that the entire manifold of moving and non-moving things (*carācara-prapañca*) is of the very nature of power. Now, in your own view...

If it is asked, "How can the manifold of the moving and the non-moving be accepted as having the nature of power (śakti), given that there is no such thing as a power residing in Brahman which could serve as its material cause?"—the answer is no. This is because [Brahman] is established by the following inference: "Brahman is qualified by being the material cause of the world, because it is the creator of the world; whatever is not so [qualified] is not so, like a jar or other such objects. Thus, by means of this inference...

A certain power, which is the material cause of the world and grounded in Brahman, is established. Furthermore, the status of being that material cause is not possible for the Pradhāna, atoms, karma, time, and so forth;
because they are insentient, it is impossible for them to be the material cause of the world. In our view, [this power resides] in Brahman.

For, by accepting a power that consists of both the conscious and the unconscious, the effect in the form of the phenomenal world (prapañca), which likewise consists of both the conscious and the unconscious, is also established; this is because it is a fixed rule that all things ending with the "unattached" (anāśrita) exist in dependence upon that [power]. And so it has been stated by the venerable Śivāditya:

(From the *Śaktisandoha*, Question 1) This entire universe, consisting of moving and non-moving beings, from Śakti down to Earth, has arisen from the union of Śiva and Śakti, just as a web arises from a spider. The Lord, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), is called the Possessor of Power (*śaktimān*). The Supreme Śakti is the nature of the attribute (*dharma-rūpā*), while the Supreme Śiva is the nature of the substratum (*dharmin-rūpaḥ*).

Because its nature is unobstructed, the supreme power of the Supreme Self always shines as His very own form, like the radiance of the sun. This identity between the two is eternal, by virtue of their natures as attribute and substratum.
In that state, Śiva exists as independent, consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss; whereas Power exists through dependence.

Therefore, [it] is accepted as the material cause of the universe. Thus, the venerable Śruti, establishing that Māyā is the material cause by stating, "One should know Māyā, the one unborn Prakṛti" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5;
4.10), [affirms] its status as such only through dependence.

It speaks of being the material cause (*upādānatva*). Therefore, since being the material cause is established through dependence, the independent Brahman’s status as the material cause is indeed established. [Material causality is defined as] the state of being a cause while being the substratum of the state of the effect, by way of either identity (*tādātmya*) or non-separation (*apṛthagbhāva*). [This applies to] the effect...

The qualifying term (viśeṣyadala) is for the purpose of excluding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to pervasion (*vyāpti*). The phrase "provided that" (*satyanta*) is for the purpose of excluding over-extension to efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*). Here, "being a substratum" (*āśrayatva*) refers to either the relation of identity (*tādātmya*) or the relation of non-separation (*apṛthagbhāva*). Thus, the definition of an efficient cause is: being a cause while being the substratum of the material cause.

The clause "being existent" (*satyantam*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the act of grasping (*upādāna*). The qualificand portion (*viśeṣyadalam*) is included to exclude [the definition's application] to the ground (*bhūtala*) and so forth, which serve as the substratum (*āśraya*) for the act of grasping; for it is not possible for the ground and such things to possess the status of being a cause (*kāraṇatva*).
This is because of them...
Because causality—in the form of being a necessary antecedent to the production of an effect—is impossible [in the case of God].

Here, "substratum-ness" (*āśrayatva*) in God is to be understood as existing through either the relation of identity (*tādātmya*) or non-separation (*apṛthagbhāva*); elsewhere, it should be understood as existing through relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), as appropriate. For [causality] consists indeed in being the substratum of the state of being an effect.
The status of power (*śakti*) as the material cause (*upādāna*) must be established.

Its very capacity extends all the way up to Brahman. Indeed, in the term *māyin* (possessing *māyā*), the suffix *-in* denotes a permanent connection; thus, by virtue of power being non-separately established from Brahman, [it constitutes its material cause].
Because even the state of being an effect, which is non-separately established from that [Brahman], can likewise be non-separately established from Brahman.
(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and so forth;
for Śakti and Śiva are expressed by the base and the suffix of the word *sat* (Being). These two, in their essential identity with Brahman, constitute the whole.

With the words "having the world as their essence" and so forth, they establish by means of the term *sat* that Supreme Śiva—who is the cause of both the efficient and material types, who is distinct from the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), and who is characterized by power (*śakti*)—consists of six stations (*ṣaṭsthala*). || 5 ||
Although the subtle power (śakti), consisting of both consciousness and non-consciousness, which rests upon Brahman,

transforms into the form of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) composed of gross conscious and unconscious entities, and Brahman itself does not transform into any form whatsoever; nevertheless, in that very manner—
Since the powers (*śakti*) residing in Brahman, as they undergo transformation,
have Brahman alone as their ultimate ground of inseparable establishment (*ayutasiddha-paryavasāna-bhūmi*),
the proof that Brahman is the material cause (*upādānatva*) up to its very limit is unimpeded. As for that which is [called] the illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of Brahman...
Māyā is that which manifests another form without abandoning its own essential nature (*svasvarūpa*);

it is the material cause (*upādāna*) by way of undergoing transformation (*pariṇāma*), which consists in abiding in another form preceded by the abandonment of its own essential nature. [This is stated] according to the maxim: "Let the wicked man be satisfied."

He refutes that [position] by following its own system, saying "that is weak. The sense is that in the non-duality of Śiva (*śivādvaite*), every entity is of the nature of existence (*sadātmaka*); therefore, there is no inconsistency whatsoever regarding the relationship between cause and effect. [The opponent says: "That is weak, because it is of the nature of existence..."
Because it is illogical to imagine that the locus of transformation (*vivartādhiṣṭhāna*) is the material cause (*upādāna*) of a phenomenal world (*prapañca*) that is unreal in nature;

for, through such statements as "The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being," one understands the negation of the relationship between material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) between the existent and the non-existent. Indeed, [this is not possible] in that which is of the nature of the existent (*sadrūpa*).

In the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), it is not accepted that the mother-of-pearl—the substratum of the illusion—is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the silver, which has an unreal form, because this would contradict experience.
Furthermore, a causal relationship is impossible between two things that do not reside in the same locus (*asamānādhikaraṇa*).
Otherwise, why should even a thread not be considered the cause of a jar? (In the Vivartavāda...)

If one accepts that silver situated in another place and time is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the mother-of-pearl standing before one, there would be no contradiction; thus, one would have to abandon the causal relationship between two entities that are co-located (*samānādhikaraṇa*) as delimited by space and time.

Since a causal relationship is admitted between two entities situated in different locations, here too a causal relationship must be admitted between the jar and the potsherds, which exist at different places and times. This being the case,

The sense is that shards and the like existing in another place and at another time would [absurdly] have to be the material cause (*upādāna*) of a jar and so forth; for in your view, shards and the like existing in another time and another place would indeed possess the status of being the material cause of a jar and so forth.

Because it is accepted that mother-of-pearl is the material cause (*upādāna*) with respect to silver, therefore the world, which is an effect consisting of *sat* (Being), must have a material cause that consists of *sat* itself; thus, Supreme Śiva alone, characterized by the power of *sat*, is the material cause. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7) "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent (*asat*); from that..."
Scriptural passages such as "Being alone was born" (sad-ajāyata) refer to the fact that during the state of dissolution,
the phenomenal world— which consists of the powers of the gross sentient and insentient—
resides within the Supreme Śiva, who is composed of the six planes and whose essential nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda).

They establish that [the universe] exists in the form of subtle powers consisting of both consciousness and non-consciousness, like seeds of grass and other plants dissolved in the earth during the summer season.
Thus it has been stated by the venerable Śivāditya (in the *Śaktisaṃdoha*, verse 1):

In such statements as "it was non-existent," the non-existence of the world is not intended; rather, it is taught that during the dissolution [of the universe], within Śiva—the supreme cause consisting of consciousness and bliss—the entire manifold of moving and unmoving things exists in a subtle form, like seeds latent in the earth during the summer heat. At that time, what is heard is the persistence of the effect in its subtle state; for the negation refers only to the effect in its manifest, causal form.

It does not exist [in the effect] by way of its causal nature; however, if it were non-existent in its entirety, then the effect would be *asatkārya* (non-existent as a cause). This is not heard there from such statements as "from that, indeed, [it arises]. Therefore, the production of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryajanana*) is proclaimed;
for in this system (the Śivādvaita Siddhānta), the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) is accepted. Thus, everything [is established].
The reality of the entire collection of effects as well as the knowledge regarding them is accepted. Now, one might object:

"Granted that the effect may be real, how can the knowledge regarding it be said to be real, since knowledge is common to both error and valid cognition (*pramā*)? This is not so; for even though knowledge is common to both error and valid cognition, [the distinction remains].
Because it is included within the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), there is no contradiction in asserting that even this [illusory object] is real.
For instance, since the cognition of similarity is real, the cognition of the rope-snake is real;
for that cognition has similarity as its object, and such a cognition is impossible without similarity.
Because the two sets of causal conditions for the visual perception that apprehends two moons— such as when the eyes are pressed by a finger—
are real, the cognition of two moons is also real. This is because,

by accepting that the effect is real due to the reality of its cause, the whiteness residing in the conch shell [is perceived as yellow] due to being obscured by the defect of bile located in one's own eye.

It is not perceived as such, like a conch shell coated with gold; therefore, even the cognition "the conch is yellow" is indeed true. Due to conjunction with various locations, various cognitions arise so rapidly that there is no awareness of the interval between them; for this reason, even the cognition of a circle of fire (ālātacakra) is true.

According to the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), since portions of the other elements also exist within each single element, water cannot be established as such because of the predominance of the space-element; thus, even the cognition of a mirage in the desert is indeed real. Furthermore, [this applies to] one who perceives the Time-Person (*kālapuruṣa*) wearing red garments, as well as a city of Gandharvas (*gandharvanagara*) in a dream.
He sees it specifically; he reaches the world of Yama within six months—of this there is no doubt.
Since such Purāṇic statements established by experience are true, even the cognition whose object is the subtle world of dreams is true; likewise,
the cognition of a magician is also truly real.
This is because the jewels, mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth that serve as its causes are real.

In this same manner, other cases should also be inferred. [Objection: But surely, since all entities other than Brahman are false—according to such statements as "Brahman is real, the world is false, and the individual soul (jīva) is indeed Brahman and nothing else"—[how can these things be real?]

If it is argued, "Why should the falsity of the categories (padārtha) stated by you not also follow?", we say no. For, according to your own logic, by the inference: "Brahman is false, because it is an object of knowledge produced by an unreal cause, like the phenomenal world (prapañca)," the falsity of Brahman itself would result. Therefore, only that which is taught in the Śivādvaita system is correct.

"Consisting of Being. Therefore, because of the relationship between material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*) between Brahman and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), the material cause of the phenomenal world—which consists of Being—is none other than Brahman itself, which consists of Being and is distinguished by its power (*śakti*); thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. || 6 ||
Furthermore, the claim that because the phenomenal world beginning with space (*viyat*) is perceived as identical with God (*īśvara*), God is therefore the material cause (*upādāna*) of it;

and likewise, because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth are perceived as identical with the individual soul (*jīva*), the individual soul alone is the material cause of these—this too is trivial. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3: "From this [Self] is born..."

Because of scriptural passages such as, "The vital breath, the mind, and all the senses; ether, air, light, water, and the earth which supports the universe," it is heard that Brahman alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious. Now, [one might object]: "In the *Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad* (2.12), [it says] 'He who is superior to the universe'..."

By such passages as "The great seer Rudra beheld Hiraṇyagarbha being born," it is established that the Supreme Lord, who transcends the universe, acts as the efficient cause through His own volition upon primordial nature (prakṛti), which is distinct from Himself.

Since it is heard in scripture that [Brahman] beholds the Golden Embryo (*hiraṇyagarbha*) being born with a glance of grace after it has been created, how can its status as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the universe be possible if it exists in the form of the supreme primordial nature (*paraprakṛti*)? For a potter, while fashioning a jar, does not himself become a lump of clay to make the jar; such a thing is impossible.

If it is argued that because it is impossible to conceive of that [Brahman], which is merely the efficient cause (*nimitta*), as the material cause (*upādāna*), and because the production of an effect is observed only through the conception of power (*śakti*) as the material cause—
then it is replied: by such passages as, "Rudra, the Great Seer, who transcends the universe, beholds Hiraṇyagarbha being born."

Just as His supremacy over the universe is understood, so too is His nature as the material cause and His universal form heard in scripture, such as in the *Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad* (24): "All is indeed Rudra," and in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* (2.14): "All this, verily, is Brahman. Furthermore, in the *Śatarudrīya*, beginning with "Obeisance to the golden-armed one... [and so forth].

By the passage ending with "Salutation to the Lord of the Kuluñcas," His lordship over the universe is heard; and then, by the passage ending with "Salutation to Parṇa and Parṇaśada," His nature as the form of the world is heard.
Therefore, Paraśiva alone, who is the efficient cause, is also the material cause. Furthermore, [in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.2]: "Thou art indeed steadfast..."

"Ask him about that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known"— by this and other such scriptural passages, it is shown that through the knowledge of the Instructor (ādeṣṭṛ), who is the instrumental cause, the entire universe consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious becomes known. Thus, [the world is known] through the knowledge of the Instructor.
Because of the proposition that "all is known" (Chāndogya 6.1.4)— namely, that "by knowing one lump of clay, all this which consists of clay becomes known"—
and because of the conformity with the illustrative example of the lump of clay provided to support that [proposition], [it follows] if Brahman were merely the efficient cause.

Through the knowledge of that [cause], the knowledge of the entire manifold of phenomena (*prapañca*) is not possible; for instance, by the knowledge of a potter, the effects such as the jar and so forth are not known, but rather [they are known] through the knowledge of the lump of clay which is their material cause (*upādāna*). Therefore...

For there is no obstacle to the fact that Paraśiva, who is the efficient cause (nimitta), is the material cause (upādāna) of the entire phenomenal world, which is a transformation of His own power that is non-distinct from Himself. || 7 ||

As for the objection that if Paraśiva, who is *saccidānanda*, is accepted as the material cause (*upādāna*), it would follow that He undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*) in the form of a modification of the cause— that is incorrect;
for Paraśiva is the cause as qualified by His subtle powers consisting of both consciousness (*cit*) and non-consciousness (*acit*).

For us, who maintain that He—distinguished by the power (*śakti*) whose nature is both gross and subtle—is the effect (*kārya*), there is no fear of such a consequence. For it is said in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* (4.18): "When there was darkness, neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being, Śiva alone existed; that was the Imperishable (*akṣara*)."

According to the Śruti, "The excellent glory of that Savitṛ, and from it the ancient wisdom has issued forth," there was a time when [the world] was devoid of the light of the moon, sun, and so forth, lacking the distinction between day and night,
and devoid of specific names and forms.

Devoid of the distinctions between gross and subtle, sentient and insentient, existent and non-existent, or manifest and unmanifest, all this existed as a state of darkness (*tamas*). At that time, Śiva alone was non-dual and solitary,
characterized by a subtle power consisting of consciousness and unconsciousness which is incapable of being divided into name and form, and he was self-luminous.

It remained as a residue. That syllable is indeed that very supreme reality which, at that time, was devoid of decay and devoid of destruction; it is that which, by previously bestowing its splendor upon the Sun (Savitṛ), is most excellent (vareṇya);
even the internal light is that same [reality]. Therefore, from such [a source]...

From that non-dual [reality], in which the entire manifold of existence— both itself and all else— has dissolved, there arises the primordial, eternally pure, great radiance of consciousness, consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśamayi*), which dispels the darkness of that time; this is the power (*śakti*) in the form of subtle consciousness and unconsciousness, which is yet to be differentiated into name and form.
It spread forth and began to flow. As it has been said by the venerable Śivāditya (in the *Śaktisaṃdoha*, Chapter 1): "From Śiva arises Power, whose nature consists of will, knowledge, and action;
endowed with immeasurable qualities, she unfolds by the command of Śiva. Here, by the word "arises," it is not meant that...

The intended meaning is this: although power possesses impermanence in the form of arising and perishing, it nevertheless undergoes a separation from the Supreme Śiva-tattva—which, like the hardness of ghee, is incapable of being divided from itself—and transforms into the form of the power of wisdom (*prajñā-śakti*), whose essence is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). || 8 ||

The Supreme Śiva-tattva, distinguished by such power of wisdom, is the Inner Controller and the cause of the universe— the Great Lord (Maheśvara)— characterized by attributes such as omniscience, eternal contentment, beginningless awakening, sovereignty, possession of undiminished power, and possession of infinite powers.

Thus it is said: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti, and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10). "Omniscience, contentment, beginningless awakening, absolute freedom, eternally undiminished power, and infinite power" (Śaktisandoha, verse 1).
Those who know the ritual procedures say that the six are the limbs of the All-pervading Maheśvara, according to such scriptural passages as [the Taittirīya Upaniṣad].

This very Maheśvara, desiring to create—as it is said in the Taittirīya (2.6), "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate'"—through the contemplation of the manifold phenomenal world, [manifested] His own power characterized as Māyā in the form of Will.

When he resorts to that power (*śakti*), being distinguished by the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), he is called Kālarudra. Then, [as stated in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6], "He performed austerity" (*sa tapo'tapyata*); thus, through the power whose nature is austerity—that is, the power consisting of knowledge (*jñāna*)—which conforms to the karma of all living beings...

When He contemplates the totality of the body and its constituents, being distinguished by the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), He is called Viṣṇu. Then, through the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*)—which is skilled in all the instruments [of creation] as conceived by His own volition—He creates this entire universe upon the foundation of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*). (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6)

When He unfolds the manifold picture of the entire universe, being then characterized by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), He is called the four-faced Brahmā. Therefore, these—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—are called the causal selves (*kāraṇātman*) because they are characterized by causal powers. As it has been said:
By the venerable Śivāditya (in the *Śaktisaṃdoha*). There, these verses [state]:

"The seed-syllable consists of primordial power (*ādiśakti*), and Śiva consists of the power of the seed-syllable (*bījaśakti*). That power is said to be threefold, consisting of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*). Endowed with this triad of powers, Sadāśiva is the creator of the universe."

The Lord Īśa possesses the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), Hari is endowed with the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), and Brahmā is endowed with the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*); these three forms have arisen in succession from Sadāśiva himself as the causal source of the universe. Previously commanded by their father, all three were assigned to three tasks: Brahmā to creation and Hari to protection.

"Likewise, Īśa is [the cause] in dissolution. Here, the meaning of "the seed consisting of primordial power" (ādiśaktimayaṃ bījam) is that Brahman, characterized by primordial power, is the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe. These three causal selves were born directly from Sadāśiva; they were previously ordained by their father.

The three [deities] are also engaged in the three activities: Brahmā in creation, Hari in protection, and Maheśa in destruction. Thus, Sadāśiva is distinguished by the power of wisdom (*prajñāśakti*), which consists of the powers of will, knowledge, and action.
As stated in the *Taittirīya Upaniṣad* (2.6): "Having created that, He entered into it."

Having created the entire aggregate of effects— characterized by the gross powers of consciousness and unconsciousness and consisting of the thirty principles beginning with *kāla* and ending with *bhūmi*, which have become transformations of its own power—
it entered into them as their very self, and thus it became both the manifest (*sat*) and the unmanifest (*tyat*). (Taittirīyopaniṣad 2.6)
The defined and the undefined, the abode and the non-abode, consciousness and unconsciousness— thus,
by virtue of being the inner controller of all and having all things as its body,
[He is] the conscious and the unconscious, the substrate and the superstratum, endowed with names common to both the perceptible and imperceptible among His own creations, and yet devoid of them.

He underwent manifold transformation into the form of the entire manifold world (prapañca), which is devoid of self-nature. Thus it is said in the *Kāraṇāgama*: "Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and likewise Śāntyatītakalā—these reside within the forms beginning with Brahmā. Indeed, by the command of Śiva, these [are established]."
Extremely brilliant beings exist there: the gods of Brahmā, the Daityas, the sages, and likewise the Manus;
all living creatures born from sweat, from eggs, and from the womb;
millions of various plants, shrubs, creepers, trees, and other beings born from sprouts; as well as mountains, rivers, and others.
The oceans and the lakes arise only in succession; therefore, the world consists of Śiva.

Thus, the definition of Brahman—the Knowable which has become the object of inquiry—is found in the Blessed Supreme Śiva, who is characterized by power (*śakti*), who is the cause of both the world and its two-fold nature, and who possesses the six stations (*ṣaṭsthala*).

By means of this systematic inquiry, it is entirely consistent that the dense *liṅga* (ghanaliṅga), whose essence is the supreme Śiva-principle (*paraśivatattva*), is precisely what those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) must desire to know. Thus ends the *Śivatattvaviveka*. [Thus ends the first chapter.]
[Now begins the second chapter.

Now, if it is asked what the *jīva* (individual soul) is and what its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is, it is replied as follows: therein, the *jīva* is that which is the object of the cognition "I," denoted by the synonym *aṅga*. Its defining characteristic, however, is that the *jīva* is characterized by the power (*śakti*) consisting of gross consciousness and non-consciousness (*cid-acid-rūpa*).

Thus [it is said in the *Śivādvaitasudhākara*]: "This individual soul (*jīva*) has the effect as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), while the Lord (*īśvara*) has the cause as his limiting adjunct. According to this statement by the learned, the gross power consisting of the sentient and insentient, which takes the form of the effect, is accepted as the limiting adjunct of the individual soul.
In order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and the liberated self (*muktātman*), the qualification "gross" (*sthūla*) is applied to the power (*śakti*).
Grossness (*sthūlatva*) consists in being characterized by the three impurities (*malatraya*); for this very reason, it is also conventionally designated as "impure" (*aśuddha*).
Furthermore, it is not logical that the gross power, which has the nature of both consciousness and non-consciousness (*cidacid-rūpa*), should be a single unity; for [if it were so]...

A doubt regarding the unity of the individual soul (*jīva*), even though it is qualified by such a power, might arise. Therefore, by accepting the plurality of that [power] in its functional form (*kāryarūpa*), the plurality of the individual soul qualified by it is also accepted; for difference is admitted through the difference of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). And this is observed in the case of a single [entity].

There is a multiplicity of the causal clay with respect to its effects—the jar, the potsherd, and so forth—as well as the specific spaces contained within them. If it is argued that this being the case, the individual soul (jīva) would consequently be limited (paricchinna), we reply: let this be granted, for such is the nature of the power consisting of the respective gross forms of the sentient and insentient.
Because it is delimited, the consciousness of the living being (*jīvacaitanya*) qualified by that [intellect] also effectively attains that [limitation].

(Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.9–10): "The part of a hundredth of the tip of a hair, further divided into a hundred parts—that part is to be known as the *jīva*; and he is fashioned for infinity. 9. Neither woman... [text truncated]
"This is a male, and not a neuter;
whatever body it assumes, with that it becomes united"—and so on, according to such scriptural passages. (1)

Now, this very power (śakti), which constitutes the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the individual soul (jīva) and consists of the gross aspects of both consciousness (cit) and the unconscious (acit), is twofold:

the power of concealment (āvaraṇa-śakti) and the power of manifestation (unmukhya-śakti). Among these, that which takes the form of a transformation of the subtle power of consciousness is conducive to the concealment of the Brahman-consciousness.

Power (*śakti*) is the power of concealment (*āvaraṇaśakti*). And its nature as concealment is the state of being fit for the conventional usage that "Brahman does not exist" or "it does not manifest. That power, resting upon the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*), becomes fivefold through the divisions of *kalā*, *vidyā*, *rāga*, *kāla*, and *niyati*. Among these, all...
The power of limited agency (*kalā-śakti*) is the form of the transformation of the power of total agency (*kartṛtva-śakti*).
The power of limited knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*) is the form of the transformation of the power of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-śakti*).
The power of attachment (*rāga-śakti*) is the form of the transformation of the power of fullness (*pūrṇatā-śakti*) into the power of incompleteness (*apūrṇatā-śakti*).
The power of impermanence (*anityatva-śakti*) is the power of time (*kāla-śakti*), which takes the form of the transformation of the power of permanence.
The power of non-pervasiveness (*avyāpakatā-śakti*) is the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*), which takes the form of the transformation of the power of pervasiveness.
Such is this pentad of powers, beginning with *kalā*, belonging to this individual soul (*jīva*).
Because it serves as the veil for one's own essential nature—which is otherwise undivided from the teaching of Paraśiva—it is called the "veiling power" (āvaraṇa-śakti);

for this very reason, it is conventionally designated as the "fivefold sheath" (pañca-kañcuka). This fivefold sheath constitutes the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) of the entire phenomenal world, which has attained both gross and subtle states.

Deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*), because the power in the form of the effect has become merged into the causal power through a state of identity (*tādātmya*). For this very reason, it is the locus of dissolution for the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) that has reached its gross and subtle states. Because it abounds in bliss (*ānanda*), it is the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*), and for this same reason, it is called the "sheath consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya-kośa*).
It is so designated. The individual soul (*jīva*) qualified by these adjuncts is called the "wise one" (*prājña*).

For the Śruti states: "The wise one (*prājña*) has deep sleep as his station; he is unified, a mass of consciousness alone, consisting of bliss, enjoying bliss, and having the mind as his gateway. (Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 5). || 2 ||

Now, the power of orientation (*aumukhyashakti*) is a subtle power of transformation of the consciousness-power (*acit-shakti*), which is conducive to the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth common to various individual souls (*jiva*). And that [power] exists by virtue of being the impeller of the supreme Śiva, whose nature is pure consciousness.

From the principle of *prakṛti* down to the principle of earth, it transforms into the nature of the twenty-four principles. In that state, from consciousness characterized by the power of *unmukhya* (orientation) which has reached the stage of the predominance of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), there arises— by way of reflection— the state of equilibrium of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, which bestow pleasure, pain, and delusion.
The principle of *prakṛti* is the fundamental cause of the twenty-three principles beginning with *buddhi* and ending with *bhūmi*.

Due to the predominance of the quality of *sattva*, the principle of *buddhi* serves as the cause of determination. Due to the predominance of the quality of *rajas*, the principle of *manas* serves as the instrument for conceptualization and doubt.
Due to the predominance of the quality of *tamas*, the principle of *ahaṅkāra* (ego) arises as the instrument for the conceit "this must be done by me.

These three [principles], residing within the body and serving as the means for directing attention toward objects of experience such as pleasure and so forth, are called the *antaḥkaraṇa* (internal organ). Thus...

From consciousness (caitanya) characterized by the emergent power (unmukhya-śakti), which has reached the stage of the predominance of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), there arises—due to the preponderance of the quality of sattva—the auditory organ (śrotra), which is the instrument for the cognition of sound attached to the external body;
the tactile organ (tvak), which is the instrument for the cognition of touch; and the visual organ (cakṣus), which is the instrument for the cognition of form.
The organ that effects the cognition of taste is called the tongue; the organ that effects the cognition of smell is called the nose.
This pentad of external organs is termed the "organs of knowledge" (*jñānendriya*) because they are characterized primarily by the power of cognition.

Thus, [the external organs arise] from consciousness (*caitanya*) as it is distinguished by the power of manifestation (*unmukhya-śakti*) which has reached the state of predominance of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
Speech is the cause of the act of utterance due to its predominance of the quality of rajas.

The hand is the instrument for actions such as giving and taking. The foot is the instrument for actions such as going and coming. The anus is the instrument for the expulsion of digested food and waste.
The organ of generation (*upastha*) is the means for the act of discharging semen and urine.
These five external organs are called "organs of action" (*karmendriya*) because they are dominated by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). This group consists of thirteen organs.
It should be understood as consisting of the powers of will, knowledge, and action. || 3 ||

Then, from consciousness characterized by the power of orientation (*unmukhya-śakti*) that has entered the state of the predominance of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), ether arises due to the predominance of the quality of darkness (*tamas*); from ether, air; from air, fire; from fire, water;
and from water, earth arise. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1: "From the Self, ether [arises]."

"From space arises air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth"—so says the Śruti. These very five *tanmātras* are called the subtle elements (*sūkṣmabhūta*). From these, both the subtle bodies (*sūkṣmaśarīra*) and the gross elements (*sthūlabhūta*) arise. [Regarding] the subtle bodies...

The five subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), the five organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*), the five organs of action (*karmendriya*), the single internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) consisting of three functions (*vṛtti*), and the single vital breath (*prāṇa*) consisting of five functions—
these seventeen components constitute what are called the *liṅgaśarīra*s (subtle bodies). In this regard:

The principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*), which is accompanied by the organs of knowledge and predominates in the power of cognition, takes the form of the agent and constitutes the sheath consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya-kośa*). The principle of mind (*manas-tattva*), which is accompanied by the organs of knowledge and predominates in the power of volition, takes the form of the instrument and constitutes the sheath consisting of mind (*manomaya-kośa*). [Likewise,] that which is accompanied by the organs of action...

The principle of *prāṇa* (vital breath), which is primarily characterized by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), becomes the sheath consisting of *prāṇa* (*prāṇamaya-kośa*) in its functional form. The union of these three sheaths is called the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*). The individual soul (*jīva*) delimited by this subtle body is designated as *taijasa*. This is the subtle body of the *taijasa*.

Because it is subtle in relation to the gross phenomenal world (*sthūlaprapañca*) and consists of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the waking state, it is called "dream" (*svapna*). For this very reason, it is the locus for the dissolution of the gross phenomenal world;
and because it is dominated by the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), it is therefore the power of knowledge itself.

It is said to consist of the three sheaths beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*). According to the Śruti: "The state of dream is the Taijasa, characterized by internal cognition, having seven limbs, nineteen mouths, and feeding on the subtle. (Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 4). 4.
The gross elements are made tripartite; "tripartition" means that among the three— fire, water, and food—
one takes each one and divides it equally into two parts, then further divides each of those portions into two, and discards its own second gross portion [of the original triad].

It is the joining together of each of the gross portions belonging to the others. For it is heard in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* (6.3.2): "This deity thought: 'Come now, let me enter these three deities with this living self and differentiate name and form. Of these [deities], she made [each] tripartite..."

"I shall make each one threefold. Now, it may be objected that once the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) has been performed, the fiery element (*taijasa*) would be perceived as possessing solidity, liquidity, and so forth, since it consists of earth and the other elements; but this is not so, because of the predominance of its own constituent part, whereby it is perceived as characterized by the qualities inherent to itself. Thus...
Since the creation of ether and air is well-known in other Vedic branches (*śākhāntara*), it is untenable to disregard it;

therefore, a synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*) is performed in order to avoid contradiction with those scriptural passages. Nor should it be said that there is no common worldly usage (*vyavahāra*) for air and ether, for we do indeed speak of "the great air" and "the great ether."

Because it is established by all experience. As for the claim that the collective quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa-samaṣṭi*) constitutes the creation of the five gross elements (*pañcabhūta*), that is not pleasing to the mind. The quintuplication of those elements that have entered the path of worldly transaction is useless, because the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) is nowhere heard of [in scripture]; rather, there would be the abandonment (*hāna*) of what is heard (*śruta*), namely the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), and the acceptance of what is unheard.

The meaning is that the theory of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) suffers from the defect of being a mere conceptual construction; for it would entail the abandonment of what is stated in scripture and the assumption of what is not stated, and it would contradict the scriptural teaching on triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*). [Objection:
But surely, by way of forming a single coherent statement with another scriptural passage, one may begin by describing the creation of the five elements...

If it is argued that the Śruti, by stating the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) of those elements as they are being treated in their subtle state for the sake of establishing worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), intends the quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), this is not so; for if that were the case,
since consistency would be achieved through tripartition alone, [the Śruti] would have taught it for the mere sake of establishing worldly transaction.

Because it is improper to conceive of a fivefold compounding (*pañcīkaraṇa*) that contradicts the Śruti; thus, even though the elements have been made tripartite (*trivṛtkṛta*), the qualities such as sound and the rest arise from their respective substrata according to their nature. This is what is meant: since ether and the other elements stand in a causal relationship toward each subsequent one, [the qualities emerge accordingly].

Because they are all-pervasive in relation to their respective effects, even though they are conjoined with the parts of those effects, they are not manifested as the substrata of the qualities residing in the effects; rather, they are manifested solely as the substrata of their own respective qualities. Likewise, because the effects are smaller than their own causes, [the qualities of the causes do not manifest in them].
Manifestation occurs even by virtue of the qualities of the cause being supported by those [effects] that are mixed with portions of the cause;
thus, from the elements made tripartite (trivṛtkṛta), there arise the fourteen worlds, the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
the fourfold gross bodies contained within it, and their appropriate [objects].

The production of food, drink, and so forth occurs [therein]. Furthermore, there are fourteen worlds: those situated one above the other, named bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ, mahaḥ, janaḥ, tapaḥ, and satya; and those situated one below the other, named atala, vitala, sutala, rasātala, talātala, mahātala, and pātāla.

The four types of bodies are known as the viviparous (*jarāyuja*), the oviparous (*aṇḍaja*), the soil-born (*udbhijja*), and the sweat-born (*svedaja*). The viviparous include humans, cattle, and so forth; the oviparous include birds, snakes, and so forth; the soil-born include trees, creepers, and so forth; and the sweat-born include worms, mosquitoes, and so forth. [The self] delimited by this gross body...

The individual soul (jīva) is called Viśva; this gross body of Viśva is the "gross body" because it is the locus for gross experience, and it is "the power of action" because it is dominated by the power of action; for this very reason, it is the waking state.
And because it is a modification of food (*annavikāra*), it is designated as the "sheath composed of food" (*annamaya-kośa*) (Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 3).
This is according to the Śruti: "The Vaiśvānara [Self] has the waking state as its domain, is conscious of external objects, has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, and is the enjoyer of the gross. (6)

Thus, that supreme Śiva-consciousness which serves as the substratum for the gross, subtle, and causal manifestations, and which is characterized by the power consisting of the subtle sentient and insentient aspects, is called the Fourth (Turya).
(Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 7: It is the cessation of the manifestation, peaceful, auspicious, and non-dual.

According to the Śruti, "They consider it the fourth," this very Fourth Consciousness (*turīyacaitanya*) is that which is denoted by the word "all" as taught in such scriptural passages as "All this, indeed, is Brahman" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 3.14.1) and "Rudra, indeed, is all" (*Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad* 16). [This refers to] the Fourth Consciousness.

First, the all-pervasive entry of Paraśivatattva is established by virtue of its being the cause of all things, according to the Vedic scripture: "Having created that, he entered into it. From that, its status as the controller of all is established, according to the Vedic scripture: "He has entered within, the ruler of people. From that...

The state of being the body of all is established because, in the *Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa*— in the passage beginning "He who dwells in the earth"— it is heard that everything in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), including the earth and so forth, which is the object of control, has the Controller as its body.
It is this very state of being the body of all that is established here, albeit indirectly, by means of the reason of being the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe.

The intended meaning is "being the self of all. And this indeed serves as the justification for the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) found in such statements as "All this, verily, is Brahman. This is evident in both worldly and Vedic usages, such as "the learned Brāhmaṇa" or "the Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava."
The sense is that words denoting a body are observed to extend to the embodied being as well. This might be argued:
it is unestablished that words denoting a body extend to the embodied being, because there is no such grammatical injunction (*anuśāsana*).
Furthermore, it is possible to account for this by the fact that both worldly and Vedic usage rely on objects established through the delusion of the body and the self.
Furthermore, there exists Vedic usage based on objects established through delusion, such as "the divine cows indeed carry [the gods] on their backs. Likewise, when the individual soul (jīva)—
which possesses the delusion of self-identity with all bodies, whether divine, human, animal, or otherwise— is considered, the statement "all this is indeed Brahman" holds true.

Thus, this designation of universal identity established through delusion is appropriate; however, one might object that it is not so in the case of the Supreme Brahman, who possesses all bodies as His own but is devoid of the delusion of identity with them. Anticipating this, he says "yathā" (just as). "Svasya" means of its own, of its own referent, namely, of the blue [object]. And so:
Words such as "blue" (nīla) and so forth denote substances qualified by qualities,

as seen in the usage of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in expressions such as "the blue lotus" (nīlam utpalam). Nor can this be accounted for through the elision of the possessive suffix *matup*, for the rule governing the elision of *matup* applies only when the suffix *matup* itself is present.
The intention is not that there is a direct denotation of the substance;

for an absence of a word cannot perform the function of a word. Nor is the intention that there is such denotation through a *matup* suffix that has been elided but is remembered, because the elision of the *matup* is for the purpose of providing a grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) of an already established word.
Since it is merely a conceptual construction of grammarians and does not exist there in reality, the *matup* suffix is actually absent;

therefore, even by the rule prescribing the elision of the *matup*, it is established that words such as "blue" (*nīla*) denote substances qualified by qualities precisely when the *matup* is not heard.

Since the elision of the *matup* suffix is taught by rule, and since the cognition of that [meaning] necessarily follows from it, the [denotation] of words such as "blue" (*nīla*) ultimately results in their being the producers of that [cognition]; so then, for what purpose is the teaching of the elision of the *matup*? For indeed, from the very usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the words "blue" and so forth—

It is established that [words] denote substances qualified by qualities. It is replied: there are words such as "blue" (*nīla*) that also denote qualities alone, since we observe even non-co-referential usages such as "the quality blue of the jar. And so, just as...

When words such as *nīla* (blue), which denote substances qualified by qualities, are intended to express the abstract quality itself, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied, resulting in forms such as *nailyam*, *nīlatvam*, and *nīlimā*. The same applies to those [words] that denote the abstract quality.

If there is an intention to express the substance (dravya) [as the possessor], the suffix *matup* may also occur; for we observe a twofold usage of words such as "merit" (*puṇya*) and "demerit" (*pāpa*), namely: "this person is meritorious," "this person is sinful," "his merit," and "his demerit."

There are two types of words denoting merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and so forth: those that denote merely the quality and those that extend to the substratum (*dharmin*) possessing that quality. When there is a desire to express the extension to the substratum for those words denoting merely the quality—such as in the usage of the *matup*-suffix in "meritorious" (*puṇyavān*) or "sinful" (*pāpavān*)—the same applies here as well, provided that [the substratum] is attained.

To exclude that [possibility], there is the instruction regarding the elision of the possessive suffix (*matup*). Consequently, words such as "blue" (*nīla*) and so forth, which ultimately denote substances, should be employed toward substances;
however, even those that terminate in the mere quality may be employed when one intends to express non-difference through metaphorical attribution (*abhedopacāra*). For example:

It is established that when there is a desire to express that what terminates in a quality alone extends as far as the substance—as in "this woman is directly the quality of blueness" or "she is blueness itself"—there is no use of the suffix *matup*. The author of the Vārttika also states: "There is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *matup* after words expressing qualities."

If it is argued that immediately after this instruction, the purpose of that [instruction] was stated as "this is established because of non-deviation" (*avyatirekāt siddham*), and that "deviation is observed," then here "non-deviation" means non-erroneousness (*avyabhicāra*); and consequently, regarding the qualities (*guṇas*) denoted by words such as "white" (*śukla*) and so forth—

The objection is that since the quality (*guṇa*) does not deviate from the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), and because the denotation of the possessor is established by the very power of words such as "white" (*śukla*), the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) for the elision of the suffix *matup* is redundant. [Response: However, in the expression "the white of the cloth" (*vastrasya śuklaḥ*), the denotation of the quality is seen to deviate from the possessor of the quality; therefore—

When there is an intention to express that a word denoting a quality alone extends up to the substance (*dravya*), the rule for elision (*luk*) is applied once the suffix *matup* would otherwise have occurred; such is the conventional usage. By this, words such as "blue" (*nīla*) and the like denote the quality alone. However, coreferential expressions such as "the blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*) rely upon the figurative treatment of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*).
The objection that this is like the grammatical designation "this is *nīlima*" is also refuted;

for if words such as *nīla* (blue), which denote a substance qualified by a quality, were to signify the quality itself, then derivative forms such as *nīlimā*, which denote the quality, would fail to be produced.
