Indeed, if the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) were applied to words denoting qualities, those words would only signify properties residing within the quality, and not [the quality itself].

The fact that [the word] denotes a quality is established. By this very [point], the resolution of the use of grammatical coordination (samānādhikaraṇa) through the two errors—the error of non-difference and the error of [superimposing] a power—is also refuted.

Nor is this a resolution that is common to unerring worldly usage. But even so, [one might object]: [Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "nanu tathāpi". The translation reflects the partial nature of the source.]

For words such as "blue" (*nīla*), which denote only a quality, the usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with respect to substances qualified by that quality is possible through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Since this is possible, no further denotative power (*śakti*) need be postulated for those [words], due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*). And thus, for the sake of restricting the scope of secondary indication—

The rule for the elision of the *matup* suffix is thus established. It follows that from words such as "blue" (*nīla*), which denote the object characterized by a quality, the formation of words like "blueness" (*nīliman*) occurs through the addition of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*); in this way, everything becomes consistent.
By this same method, words denoting the body—such as "god," "human," and "brahmin"—also extend in their denotation up to the self (*ātman*). And it is not otherwise.
It should not be argued that, in that case, words such as "body" (śarīra) would also refer to the Self;

for the ground for the application (pravṛttinimitta) of those terms— namely, "bodiness" (śarīratva)— is its being the locus of that which is directly non-separate from itself, just as is the case with words such as "god" (deva) or "human" (manuṣya).

Because for those [words], in order to prevent an over-extension resulting from the absence of application up to the self (ātman), the qualification "directly" (sākṣāttva) is necessary; therefore, since words such as "blue" (nīla) etc.
are seen to extend up to the substance (dravya), by that same principle, words denoting the phenomenal world (prapañca) also extend up to Brahman.

This is appropriate; for, as in the case of "the blue jar" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*) and so forth, we observe such usages as "Śarva is indeed Rudra" (*śarvo vai rudraḥ*), and thus these [words] are identical to words such as "blue" (*nīla*). Here, this should be understood: regarding those words...

The capacity [of a word] exists merely in that which is the locus of its own primary etymological occasion (pravṛttinimitta); it is upon these that the application of the logic of words such as "blue" (nīla) is based. For those [theorists] for whom the qualification of "directness" (sākṣāttva) is required in the capacity [of the word] with respect to its locus, there is no denotation of Brahman.

This is established by the same logic as the word "blue" and so forth; however, the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in such passages as "Śarva is indeed Rudra," as well as the resolve to become manifold and the differentiation of names and forms, are established by [these] authoritative means.
For this very reason, the author [uses] the word "Śarva" not merely...

Furthermore, since words such as "blue," "red," and "human" denote not only the manifold of moving and non-moving things but also the Śiva-principle qualified by them— because they denote universals that are inseparably established in their substrates— it has been established that Brahman is denotable by all words. And thus, regarding words such as "form" (rūpa) and so forth...

The established position is that power (*śakti*) resides in the substratum itself, just as in the case of the power of words such as "blue" (*nīla*). This [definition] is intended merely to exclude that [power] from extending to objects such as a jar (*ghaṭa*), lest it do so;

however, the power of Brahman—established by scriptural passages such as those concerning the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*)—is not excluded in that way. Thus, everything [is consistent].
It is consistent. Just as the word "blue" denotes not only itself but also the lotus qualified by it,
so too the word "all," which denotes the entire manifold of moving and non-moving things, denotes not only that manifold but also [the Self] qualified by it.

But since that [quality] belongs to the Śiva-tattva as well, which is distinguished by it, he therefore cites the statement from the *Vāyusaṃhitā*—which establishes that [Brahman] is denotable by all words by demonstrating the characteristics of Brahman’s body: "The body" (*vigraham*). The word "body" (*vigraham*) is used in the Vedic style (*chāndasa*).

There is a change of gender. By this verse, the fact that the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) in general is the body of the Supreme Lord is shown. By the second verse, the fact that its specific constituents—consisting of both sentient and insentient beings—are His body is shown. In the second half of that [verse]:
By stating, "It is form indeed, there is no doubt," it is shown that the world's being the body of That (Brahman) is primary and not merely figurative. To demonstrate this,
after first indicating the definition of a body, [it is shown that] its persistence within the world exists, for the universe is under His control.

By this statement, [the definition] is demonstrated. By this, it is indicated that the defining characteristic of a body (*śarīra*) is being subject to control (*niyamyatva*), in the form of being under another's power.
To exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to cases such as a master and his servant—who also exercises control through pervasion—the phrase "he who controls by pervading" [is included].

The phrase "that is His body" provides the definition of Him; this is further refined by the qualification in the second half [of the verse], where the term "all-pervading" (vibhuḥ) declares His pervasion of the entire manifold universe subject to His control.
It is precisely with this intention that even the etymological derivation of His eight names becomes consistent.
"Śiva presides over and pervades everything from the principle of Śakti down to the earth, and from the earth up to objects such as a jar;
therefore, he is declared to be Viṣṇu. Thus, the Master, remaining unattached, governs his servants, just as a boatman, having boarded his boat, governs it while remaining distinct from it.
It exists in only one part [of that object]. A man who is a "false tiger"—

having entered a mechanical device made of wood, leather, or other materials fashioned in the shape of a tiger— does not occupy or pervade it even while controlling it, because his hands, feet, and so forth remain in a state of separation.

Even though [the soul] sometimes presides over [the body] by means of instigation and so forth, it does not do so by pervading [it]; thus, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to those [other things]. However, since hands, feet, and so on, when they have attained a particular state consisting of a specific mutual conjunction, are indeed the body itself, and are therefore the very objects to be defined (*lakṣya*), there is no over-extension to them either.

Since the group of vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and sense organs is also included within the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to them either. Transmigrating beings (*saṃsārin*) govern [their bodies] by pervading the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), governing without presiding over the parts of their own bodies that are to be governed. Liberated beings (*mukta*), however, [govern] solely through the pervasion of the power of consciousness.

Since they govern by presiding over the universe, there is no lack of pervasiveness (avyāpti) anywhere. Furthermore, this [characteristic]—like the definition of Brahman as the "origin, etc., of the world"—is an occasional indicator (upalakṣaṇa) and not a defining attribute (viśeṣaṇa). Therefore, the fault that a body in deep sleep would incur the status of being a "body" [does not apply].

There is no such possibility. And this being the case, it is not a defect that while Caitra continues to preside over liberation, his body would likewise result in being a body for him even during the state of saṃsāra; for such a consequence is accepted. For this very reason, [the objection regarding] the limited sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) which has as its object only the human body and so forth—

The nature of being an error is thus established. To indicate this very definition of a body, the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa—beginning with "He who dwells in the earth," and so forth—first demonstrates the Supreme Lord's pervasion both externally and internally within the earth and other elements, and then declares that the earth and the rest are subject to His control. Therefore:
Nor is there any loss of the identity between the word "Brahman" as heard [in scripture] and the word "all" (sarva),

because the grounds for the application of words denoting the phenomenal world (prapañca) apply equally— whether directly or indirectly— to that which is merely the inseparable substrate of its own locus.
Since the status of being the ground for the application of words has been established,

and since there is no difference in the grounds for the application of any word with respect to both the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and Brahman as the denotable objects, [the statement] indicates the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) of the phenomenal world and Brahman.

However, the status of the two words as being either the first or the last in the sentence must be set aside for the sake of conforming to the Vedic revelation (*brahma-śruti*), because they take the form of a sentence and a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Even though the particle *iti*— which provides the reason for the meaning already stated in the passage "All this, indeed, is Brahman" (*sarvaṃ khalvidaṃ brahma*)— is itself a Vedic word, within a sentence that contains the Vedic revelation of Brahman, [the former status must yield].
In view of the initial application [of the suffix], the causality of that object must be stated by means of the particle *iti*; thus,
for the sake of favoring the primary application of the Vedic word *brahman*, when it is established that Brahman is the body of all, by that [fact],
everything cognizable through the same consciousness as Him is likewise the body of Brahman.
It should be established that [the Lord] is spoken of as the cause; enough of this digression.

The world of moving and non-moving beings is the body of the God of gods; beasts do not understand this truth due to the weight of their fetters. They call consciousness "knowledge" (vidyā) and unconsciousness "ignorance" (avidyā).

The entire universe, consisting of both knowledge and ignorance, is the form of this all-pervading Guru of the universe; of this there is no doubt, since the universe is under his control. The word *sat* is used by the virtuous for that which is real and good, while the word *asat* is spoken by those who proclaim the Vedas for its opposite. Thus, the entire universe is both *sat* and *asat*.

"The body of the Supreme Self. Regarding this, it should be understood as follows: the collection of the four types of gross bodies (*sakala-sthūla-śarīra*) which constitute the locus of experience; the objects of enjoyment such as food and drink;
the fourteen worlds beginning with Bhūr which constitute that locus; and the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) which constitutes that locus.
All of this— the gross manifestation (*sthūla-prapañca*), the subtle elements that serve as its cause, and the collection of subtle bodies—
all of these consist of the nature of the gross, insentient power (*acetana-śakti*).
The cause of this is the pentad beginning with *kalā*, which stands in the position of the archetype (*bimba*).

And all this that has arisen from the causal body (kāraṇa-śarīra) consists of the nature of gross conscious power. Therefore, because it is governed by Paraśiva—who has attained a state of pervasiveness throughout this entire phenomenal world (prapañca) composed of both the sentient and the insentient—all of this is indeed of the very form of His body. And such being the case, there is no [defect] for Paraśiva...

It should not be argued that there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of the individual soul (*jīva*) to the case of [the Lord] being qualified by the powers of gross consciousness and unconsciousness;

for since "qualification" (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is accepted as involving a specific type of relation, that defect can be avoided. In the definition [of the individual soul], the relation is either identity with itself (*svatādātmya*) or non-separation (*apṛthagbhāva*); however, in this case [of the Lord],...
The relationship [consists] of ownership and so forth. || 7 ||

Thus, because this individual consciousness (jīvacaitanya) is characterized by powers in the form of the gross material and immaterial universe— from the level of *kalā* up to the level of *bhūmi*— through a relationship of either identity with or non-separation from its own self,
it possesses the attributes of being the agent of all, omniscience, fullness, eternity, and omnipresence.
The subtle powers become contracted;

therefore, when its power of will (*icchā-śakti*), whose nature is unimpeded sovereignty, becomes contracted, it is called the *āṇava-mala*, which consists of the state of thinking oneself incomplete. When the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) is contracted...

The impurity of Māyā is said to be that which consists in the manifestation of duality and knowable objects, arising from the connection with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the sense organs, due to the attainment of limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*) instead of omniscience (*sarvajñatva*). In this way, the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), being contracted, [is called the impurity of Karma].

Because the state of being the agent of all things attains the status of being an agent of only some things due to the influence of connection with the organs of action (*karmendriya*), it is called the "karma-mala," consisting of the performance of auspicious and inauspicious deeds. Thus it has been stated by the venerable Śivāditya: "Consciousness, when afflicted by *mala*, relies upon *kalā* and *vidyā*..."
With its self colored by passion, likewise measured by time, further restrained by necessity (niyati),

and augmented by the state of being a person (puṃbhāva); endowed with the latent impressions of primordial matter (pradhāna), possessed of the three qualities (guṇa), seated upon the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva), enveloped by the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and [joined] with the mind (manas).
"They call the individual soul (jīva) that which is conjoined with the intellect, the organs of action, the sense organs, the subtle elements (tanmātras), and the gross elements;

its characteristic is being enveloped by transmigratory existence. Therefore, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in applying the definition—consisting in being characterized by the power (śakti) whose nature is the gross form of both the conscious and the unconscious—to the individual soul when it is distinguished by the three impurities (malas) and tormented by the miseries of transmigratory existence.
The opportunity for such faults is to be discerned by the wise themselves. Thus ends the *Jīvatattvaviveka*.
[Thus ends the second chapter.]
[Now begins the third chapter.

Thus, the distinction between Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) has been described by way of the differentiation of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of the powers (*śakti*) that take the form of the subtle and gross universe. Now, their non-dual nature as Śivādvaita is being described.

Regarding the term *śivādvaita*, by the force of its etymological derivation— where *śiva* and *śiva* are two *śivas*, and the non-duality (*advaita*) of those two is *śivādvaita*— the first word *śiva* conveys Brahman as qualified by the subtle power (*śakti*) consisting of both consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*). The other word *śiva*...

The term "gross" (*sthūla*) denotes the individual soul (*jīva*) as qualified by the power (*śakti*) whose nature is both conscious and unconscious; and the term "non-dual" (*advaita*) denotes the non-difference between those two. Thus, by virtue of the transformation of its own power, [the Self], being delimited by the three bodies through connection with the three impurities (*mala*), acts under the influence of concealing its own true nature.

The supreme Śiva-tattva, having attained the state of the individual soul (jīva), becomes by its own nature full with the essence of the bliss of its own true form—being no longer delimited by the three bodies due to the removal of the three impurities (mala) through the expansion of its own power; thus, an absolute difference between the two is not tenable. And so it has been said:
"Consciousness is the nature of the Self, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss; since its nature is unobscured, by whom can its state of Śiva-hood be prevented? (1)

Nor should it be argued that since Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) are perceived as characterized by mutually contradictory powers, an absolute difference between them is established, and thus their non-difference cannot be logically maintained;
for it is Śiva, qualified by subtle powers consisting of both consciousness (cit) and the unconscious (acit), who possesses the status of the cause.
In our view, which maintains that the cause is characterized by the power (*śakti*) consisting of gross consciousness and unconsciousness (*cid-acid-rūpa*),

the absolute difference between cause and effect is utterly rejected because it results in their non-difference (*abheda*). Furthermore, an absolute difference between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its product (*upādeya*) has never been observed, whether in terms of being a lump of clay or a jar.

For even though there is a difference between the lump of clay and the jar, there is a universal recognition of their non-difference by virtue of both being made of clay; and because the relationship of material cause and effect (upādānopādeyabhāva) is accepted between the qualified whole and its qualified state, as well as between the qualifier and its own qualifier.

For it is possible to realize the non-difference even between those respective powers; nor is it logical that there should be a difference between the two powers as qualified by them, on the grounds of a difference between their delimiters— namely, subtlety and grossness—
since their non-difference is ultimately established by virtue of their consisting of both consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*).

Therefore, regarding the acceptance of the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman: [Muṇḍakopaniṣad 3.1.1]—herein lies the intention. In the scriptural text "Two birds," the difference between the individual soul and Brahman is indeed established; likewise, it is said that "two Brahmans are to be known: the higher and the lower."
The same applies here as well: in passages such as "Brahman is indeed one without a second; there is no diversity whatsoever here;

other than this, there is no seer; other than this, there is no hearer," and in "Rudra is indeed one; he does not stand for a second," and in "where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else," and so forth.

Since the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is established [in some texts], while other scriptural passages contradict it, one cannot maintain either dualism alone or monism alone;
rather, one must accept the position of *Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita* (Qualified Non-dualism), which consists of both duality and non-duality. Its meaning is as follows:

"Śakti" and "śakti" [make] "śaktī"; those two, distinguished by their powers, are "śaktiviśiṣṭe" (distinguished by power); the non-duality of those two is "śaktiviśiṣṭādvaitam" (non-duality qualified by power). Here, by the first word "śakti," the power in the form of the subtle world-complex consisting of consciousness and the unconscious is denoted; by the other word "śakti,"...

The power (*śakti*) that takes the form of the manifold (*prapañca*) consisting of gross consciousness and non-consciousness is so called. By the term "qualified by those two powers," Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*) are denoted. The established doctrine (*siddhāntasvarūpa*) is that there exists non-duality—that is, oneness—between these two; that is to say, between that which is qualified by power in its subtle state and that which is qualified by power in its gross state.

The Supreme Śiva-tattva alone is the internal controller (antaryāmin) who is the primary regulator; because He exists as the conscious internal controller within all conscious individual souls (jīvas), scriptural statements such as "There is no other seer than Him" and "Nothing else hears [anything] but Him" are logically established in relation to Him.

Just as the linguistic usage "Devadatta alone is now in his own house" proceeds even though Devadatta is characterized by a multiplicity of things such as body and sense organs, so too is the statement "Brahman is one only, without a second" established. Furthermore, the verse "Two birds... is naturally established [as referring to the individual soul and the Supreme Self]; thus, he says that there is no contradiction with any scripture whatsoever.
"Because there is no contradiction. [The Śruti says: "Two birds, companions and friends, cling to the same tree.
Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating. Two.

If one were to accept duality in contradiction with such statements establishing difference as "Two Brahmans are to be known, the higher and the lower," then it would conflict with the scriptural texts:
"Brahman is one only, without a second"; "There is no diversity whatsoever here"; "Rudra is indeed one;
he does not stand for a second"; and "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else—that [is Brahman]."
Furthermore, because both [the Advaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita positions] would result in invalidity due to contradiction with the sentence "Thou art That," which enjoins non-difference,
the position of Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita alone must be accepted; for in this position,

the non-dualistic texts are understood by taking the non-difference between the two [Brahman and the world] as qualified by power (śakti), which manifests in the form of the subtle and gross categories of consciousness and unconsciousness.
For there is no contradiction, since the authority of even non-dual (advaita) statements is established by taking recourse to the distinction between the qualifier and the qualified. || 2 ||
Granted that non-duality may be established between cause and effect by taking their identity as a basis, however,

it is impossible to realize the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is delimited by the three bodies, with Śiva, who is not so delimited. Even if there were such a realization of identity...

The difference between the delimitors of the qualifier (*prakāratāvacchedaka*) and the delimitors of the qualificand (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*) is also a necessary condition [for the cognition of identity]. For example, in the case of "the blue pot," there is a difference between blueness and potness. For this very reason, in cases such as "the pot is a pot," there is no cognition of identity; thus, the difference between the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman does not contradict the cognition of their non-difference.
Nevertheless, it remains consistent with the direction previously stated. Even so,

because the omniscience and limited-knowledge status residing in those two [Brahman and the individual soul] are mutually contradictory— being based respectively on their being delimited by various entities such as body and senses, and their being undelimited— the definition characterized by the exclusion of partial attributes (*bhāgatyāga-lakṣaṇā*) is adopted.

If it is argued that, even though "blueness" (*nīlatva*) and "potness" (*ghaṭatva*) are distinct, there is no need for such a definition because they lack mutual contradiction (*viruddhatva*), since their absolute difference is unavoidable due to their possible coexistence— then it is replied: [as will become clear later].
(He connects [the argument] by means of an illustration, beginning with "just as":

Just as, although a distinction is established for the ether delimited by limiting adjuncts such as a jar or a hut due to the difference between those adjuncts, the realization of its non-difference from the great ether that is not so delimited is nonetheless established; so too [is it here].

Even if the differentiation of the individual consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*)—as delimited by this or that body—is established through the difference between those respective bodies, the realization of non-difference from Śiva-consciousness, which is not so delimited, remains logically tenable.
Thus it is heard in the *Vātulottara*: "Just as space is perceived [as distinct] through the breaking of various large jars."

Thus, a single locus is understood through the distinction between the mark (*liṅga*) and its parts (*aṅga*). Here, it should be understood according to the previously stated direction that the essential nature (*svarūpa*), which consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*),

is characterized by its own essence as being qualified by a subtle power (*śakti*) composed of both the conscious and the unconscious (*cid-acit*), which is incapable of division into name and form (*nāma-rūpa*).

That supreme Śiva-consciousness, which is characterized by the origin and so forth of the entire universe, which is distinct from all things, and which is the self of all—that is designated by the word *sthala*. It is called *sthala* because it is that wherein everything stands (*tiṣṭhati*) and dissolves (*līyate*); it is the eternal Brahman, the infinite support of all, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*).
And because of scriptural statements such as: "That state in which the phenomenal world (prapañca) dissolves into Brahman is known as [the causal state].
When that Supreme Śiva-consciousness becomes qualified by the subtle powers of both the conscious and the unconscious, which are fit for the differentiation of name and form, then—
The nature and essence of the twenty-five auspicious *līlā* forms, characterized by being Virūpākṣa, Kṛṣṇapiṅgala, Nīlakaṇṭha, and so forth;
that which is denoted by the eight names beginning with Bhava, Śiva, Sarva, Mahādeva, and Parameśvara; and [the state of] omniscience.

The reality of Maheśvara is said to be characterized by unique attributes consisting of eternal satisfaction, primordial consciousness, the possession of sovereign power (*tatantra-śaktimatva*), the possession of undiminished power (*alupta-śaktimatva*), and the possession of infinite power (*ananta-śaktimatva*).
When the powers of this Maheśvara, such as omniscience and the rest, undergo transformation in the form of *kalās*.

This is what is expressed by the term *liṅga*. Thus, the individual soul (*jīva*), characterized by the power of the gross forms of consciousness and matter, through the ripening of its own karma produced by meritorious deeds accumulated over many births— and having destroyed the latent impressions of impurity—
by the power of Śiva’s grace generated through the constant performance of Śiva-worship, Śiva-conduct, and so forth, [attains liberation].

When the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) becomes pure, then the powers of this individual soul (*jīva*), such as limited knowledge and limited agency, transform into the form of devotion (*bhakti*). At that time, he [the author] states that this [soul] is designated by the term "limb" (*aṅga*) in the phrase "this soul. Here, this must be considered: regarding the word "limb" (*aṅga*)...

Although the word "body" (śarīra) is used here by its conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*) to denote a physical frame, since the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa*— in such passages as "he whose body is the self" and "he whose body is the unmanifest"— teaches that the entire range of entities from the earth up to the individual soul (*jīvātman*) constitutes the body of Brahman, the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is also denotable by the term "limb" (*aṅga*).

There is no inconsistency whatsoever. By this very same reasoning, just as the conventional usage of Brahminhood and non-difference from a Brahmin occurs with respect to the Self through the body of a Brahmin, so too the conventional usage of the non-difference of the individual soul (jīvātman) from Brahman—by means of the individual soul which has become the body of Brahman—is not inconsistent; such is the truth.
The individual soul (jīva) is denoted by the word "limb" (aṅga). This very soul, denoted by the word "limb,"—

by virtue of the descent of the power of Maheśvara arising from the influence of devotion to Śiva— becomes the inner self (pratyagātman) distinct from the body and other such things, and is proficient in the discernment between the Self and the non-Self through the thought "I am."

Considering the perishability of the pleasures derived from sense objects such as garlands, sandalwood paste, and women, as well as the perishability of the bliss of heaven and so forth produced by sacrifices like the Jyotiṣṭoma,
and perceiving the worthlessness of this saṃsāra defiled by the sufferings of birth, death, and the like, [he abandons] attachment to saṃsāra.
He renounces [the world]. Thus, the living soul (jīva), having attained the state of being a fit vessel through the realization of the unity of the individual and the universal,
and desiring to know the Supreme Brahman— which is the destroyer of saṃsāra and is denoted by the term "dense-liṅga" (ghanaliṅga)—
approaches with offerings in hand one who knows the reality of the Śiva-siddhānta and who dispels the doubts of disciples.

Having approached the venerable Śrī Guru— who is independent in all scriptures, born of a lineage of teachers, the expounder of the knowledge distinguished by the eight coverings, the revealer of the secret of the identity of the *liṅga* and the *aṅga*, learned in the Vedas, and established in Brahman— he follows him.

"Having examined the worlds acquired through karma, a Brahmin should attain detachment, realizing that 'there is nothing uncreated [attained] by means of the created. For the sake of knowing That, he should approach a Guru alone, carrying fuel in his hand—one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman. Thus says the Śruti. Now...
That glorious Guru, an ocean of compassion, out of supreme grace initiated his own disciple— who had come into his presence and was endowed with all auspicious marks— into the Śiva-initiation; first,
by means of the piercing initiation (*vedhadīkṣā*) consisting of the joining of his hand with the disciple's head.
Having joined the *bhāvaliṅga* to the individual soul (*jīva*) as delimited by the *kāraṇāṅga*, which has another name, *yogāṅga*;

and having joined the *prāṇaliṅga* to the individual soul as delimited by the *sūkṣmāṅga*, which has another name, *bhogāṅga*, by means of the initiation consisting of the instruction of the great five-syllabled mantra;

Having first performed the installation of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the five jars (*pañcakalaśa*), and so forth, and having joined the *iṣṭaliṅga* to the individual soul (*jīva*)— which is delimited by the gross limb known by the other name "the limb of renunciation" (*tyāgāṅga*) through the ritual initiation consisting of the arrangement of the *śivakalā*s—
and having established the form of the *śivaliṅga* within the individual self (*jīvātman*) preceded by the deposition of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), [one should perform the rite] upon the *liṅga*.
Having taken up the life-force of the disciple, the teacher carries away the chosen *liṅga* of that disciple;
having pointed out the chosen *liṅga* as being held in the disciple's hand— like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand—
he indicates it.

By means of the distinction between knowledge and action as taught in the Siddhānta scriptures— which encompass the six stages and contain within them the one hundred and one unsurpassed stages (*sthala*) that are the supreme means for attaining liberation in the form of identity with the dense *liṅga* (the supreme reality), being distinguished by the five modes of conduct (*pañcācāra*) and the eight enclosures (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*) well-known from all the Vedas, Āgamas, and Purāṇas.

With a mind entirely absorbed in the threefold forms of worship— the *mūrti-liṅga*, the *prāṇa-liṅga*, and the *bhāva-liṅga*— which consist of the sixfold divisions based on the support of the contemplation of the objects of the hand, the mantra, the face, the limbs, the signs (*liṅga*), and the power (*śakti*) that serves as the mode for presenting the category of form (*rūpa*).
In the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* (1.2.13), he teaches the non-dual knowledge of Śiva— also known as the identity of the *liṅga* and the *aṅga*:

"To him who had approached him, whose mind was perfectly tranquil and who was endowed with self-restraint, that wise one fully declared that knowledge of Brahman in accordance with reality, by which one knows the imperishable, true Person."
On account of scripture. || 3 ||

Now, the method for realizing the secret of the identity (*sāmarasya*) between the *liṅga* and the *aṅga* (that is to say, the state of being of one essence, the mutual and eternal connection between Śiva and the individual soul) is described.
To this end: the *ghanaliṅga*, which is the very nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and is also known by the name of the supreme reality (*paraśivatattva*), [is as follows].

Through the differentiation of the *kalās* which are the transformations of its own power (*svaśaktipariṇāma*), it becomes threefold: being qualified by the *sattā-kalā*, it is the *bhāvaliṅga*; being qualified by the *cit-kalā*, it is the *prāṇaliṅga*; and being qualified by the *ānanda-kalā*, it is the *iṣṭaliṅga*. Furthermore, these three *liṅgas* [are distinguished] by the internal differentiation of their respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Each one is of two kinds; therein, the *bhāvaliṅga* is distinguished by the *kalā* beyond the *śāntātīta*, while the *mahāliṅga* is distinguished by the *kalā* of *śāntātīta*. The *prasāda*—

The *liṅga* is of two kinds. The *prāṇaliṅga* is distinguished by the *śāntikalā*, while the *jaṅgamaliṅga* is distinguished by the *vidyākalā*. Thus, there are two [other] types: the *iṣṭaliṅga*, which is distinguished by the *pratiṣṭhākalā*, and the *guruliṅga*, which is distinguished by the *nivṛttikalā*.

The *ācaraliṅga* is of two kinds. Thus it has been said in the *Vātulāgama*: "That which is the dense *liṅga* (*ghanaliṅga*), possessing great luster, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss, partless, actionless, tranquil, independent, and self-luminous, [is the *ācaraliṅga*] because it serves as the locus for all things."

Because it is the locus of dissolution, it is likewise called the "place" (*sthala*) of the principles beginning with *mahat*. That Brahman in which the phenomenal world dissolves—the immovable, infinite support of all, whose nature is being, consciousness, and bliss—is known as the "place. By the mere agitation of its own power, that place is twofold.
It may be so. One is declared to be the station of the *liṅga* (*liṅgasthala*), while the other is remembered as the station of the limbs (*aṅgasthala*).

The station of the *liṅga* should be known as threefold, according to the distinction between the *bhāva-liṅga*, the *prāṇa-liṅga*, and the *iṣṭa-liṅga*. The first would be the *bhāva-liṅga*, the second the *prāṇa-liṅga*, and the third would be the *iṣṭa-liṅga*; thus it is threefold.

It is taught: Each single site is further of two kinds, and each of those two is of two kinds. The Mahāliṅga is called Prasāda; that which arises from the division of Bhāvaliṅga is called Jaṅgama, born from Prāṇaliṅga;
and the Śivaliṅga is distinguished [from these]. Likewise, the Guruliṅga and Ācāraliṅga are distinguished according to their respective preferences. Thus it is said.

Thus, the stage of the limbs (*aṅga*) denoting the individual soul (*jīva*) becomes threefold according to the distinctions of its own inherent adjuncts of devotion: the limb of yoga (*yogāṅga*) characterized by pure devotion (*viśuddhabhakti*), the limb of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*) characterized by investigative devotion (*vicārabhakti*), and the limb of renunciation (*tyāgāṅga*) characterized by prescriptive devotion (*vidheyabhakti*).
Furthermore, these three limbs are each of two kinds according to the distinction between the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of devotion residing within oneself (*svagata*). Among them,
the limb of yoga (*yogāṅga*), characterized by devotion of equal flavor (*samarasa*), is the stage of unity (*aikyasthala*).
The stage of refuge (*śaraṇasthala*) is twofold, being characterized by the devotion of bliss (*ānandabhakti*). The limb of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*) is twofold:

the stage of the *prāṇaliṅgin* characterized by the devotion of experience (*anubhavabhakti*), and the stage of the *prasādin* characterized by the devotion of attentiveness (*avadhānabhakti*). [The limb of renunciation (*tyāgāṅga*)...]

The stage of Maheśvara is distinguished by ultimate devotion (*naiṣṭhika-bhakti*), while the stage of the devotee (*bhakta-sthala*) is distinguished by faith and devotion (*śraddhā-bhakti*); thus, it is of two kinds. As it has been said by the teachers who perceive the subtle: "The stage of the limbs (*aṅga-sthala*) is likewise proclaimed; the first is called the limb of yoga (*yogāṅga*), and [the second] the limb of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*)."
The second is the limb of renunciation (*tyāgāṅga*), and the third is the limb of yoga (*yogāṅga*); thus it is remembered as being threefold.

Oneness (*aikya*) and the state of refuge (*śaraṇasthala*) constitute the two-fold limb of yoga. The two—the one who bears the *liṅga* of breath (*prāṇaliṅgin*) and the one who is graced (*prasādī*)—are considered the limb of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*). The state of the Great Lord (*māheśvarasthala*) and the state of the devotee (*bhaktasthala*) constitute the two-fold state.
"It is declared by the seers of reality that this indeed becomes a factor of renunciation. (5)
Thus, in this context, because it is the benefactor, the *liṅga* aspect is the object of worship;
because it is the beneficiary, the *aṅga* aspect becomes the worshipper.

Since meditation is the cause for the cessation of dualistic perception, there is a falling away [of duality] between those two—the *liṅga* and the *aṅga*—which have attained the state of the worshipped and the worshipper.

The meaning is that, according to the analogy of the *marakīṭaka* (the bee-insect), there is non-difference [between the individual soul and Śiva]; just as an insect absorbed in meditation on a bee becomes a bee itself, so too a living being (*jīva*) absorbed in meditation on Śiva becomes Śiva himself. Thus, the point is that in the state of liberation (*mokṣa*), there is indeed non-difference between the two. And so it has been said: "Just as by union with a bee, even an insect..."
"A human being acts like a bee; likewise, through the yoga of Śiva, he becomes Śiva himself.

The yogi devoted to the yoga of Śiva is indeed Śiva—of this there is no doubt. (Thus it is stated in the Āgamas. He shall remain in this very state. And [there is no identity] of the individual soul (*jīva*), denoted by the term "limb" (*aṅga*) when delimited by the three bodies, with that which is not delimited by the three bodies.

It should not be asked how non-difference with Śiva, who is denoted by the word *liṅga*, can be established; for [it is said]: "The *liṅga*, facing in all directions, is well-established everywhere and at all times within the self through the instruction of the Guru in all its limbs."
"Then, for that conscious being, [the light] shines continuously"— by this statement from the *Vātulottara*,

and by the venerable Guru’s [teaching] that "this Guru, having burnt away the three beginningless impurities (*mala*) residing in the three bodies of this living being (*jīva*) through the three initiations (*dīkṣā*), taught the three marks (*liṅga*)," as stated in the *Divyāgama*, [he acts].
Having removed the three impurities (mala), through the connection with the three *liṅgas* established within the three bodies,

this [soul] consists of the *liṅga* in all its limbs; thus, since everything in all the senses and all the bodies becomes composed of the *liṅga*, what room is there for the suspicion that it is limited by the three bodies?
Just as the *liṅga*, though delimited by the three bodies (*śarīra-traya*) in its aspect as *kalā*, remains undelimited by them;

so too the *aṅga*, though delimited by the three bodies in its aspect as *bhakti*, remains undelimited by them. And thus it is heard in scripture: "Bhakti is indeed remembered as Śakti, and Śakti is always indeed Bhakti."

In the investigation of ultimate reality, there is no difference between *śakti* (power) and *bhakti* (devotion). *Śakti* is declared to be activity (*pravṛtti*), while *bhakti* is said to be cessation (*nivṛtti*). Through *śakti*, the creation of the phenomenal world occurs; through *bhakti*, its dissolution is held to take place. Indeed, by virtue of its manifold variety, *śakti* assumes form even though it is formless; likewise, by virtue of its manifold variety, *bhakti*...

Even form would attain the state of formlessness. For the natural quality of *śakti* (power) is the expansion of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), while the natural quality of *bhakti* (devotion) is the dissolution of the phenomenal world. *Śakti* becomes downward-facing, whereas *bhakti* becomes upward-facing. *Śakti* is said to be accompanied by *māyā*, while *bhakti* is free from *māyā*.
Devotion has been described. Even by means of logic and valid cognition, devotion is superior to power (*śakti*).

Through power there may be the state of being the object of worship, but through devotion there arises the state of being the worshiper. Therefore, power resides in the place of the *liṅga*, while devotion resides in the place of the limbs (*aṅga*). The place of the *liṅga* is Śiva himself in person.

"The locus of the individual soul (jīvātman) shall be the locus of the limbs; for the identity of the limbs of the *liṅga* and the limbs [of the body] is indeed the identity of Śiva and the individual soul. Thus [it is said]. (6)

If it is asked, "How can the soul's possession of all three *liṅgas* be established according to the method you have stated, given that the three *liṅgas* are joined to the three bodies at some unspecified location?"— it is replied:
even though the three *liṅgas* are joined to the three bodies at some unspecified location, those three *liṅgas*...

Having become sixfold through the divisions of the *mahāliṅga* and so forth, it remains pervading all the limbs. In this manner, one should understand that the application of each respective *liṅga* occurs sequentially for all the sense organs as well. As it has been said:
"The *ācāraliṅga*, known as the nose, is situated in the station of the devotee (*bhakta*) and is endowed with the *nivṛtti-kalā*."

The means for perceiving smell is the Guru-liṅga, known as the tongue; it rests upon the station of Māheśa and is endowed with the power of Pratiṣṭhā, serving as the instrument for perceiving taste. The Śiva-liṅga, known as the eye, rests upon the station of Prasāda and is endowed with the power of Vidyā, serving as the instrument for perceiving form.

The mobile liṅga called *tvak* (skin) is located in the station of *prāṇaliṅgin*; it is endowed with the *śānti* kalā and is the instrument for perceiving touch. The *prasādaliṅga* called *śrotra* (ear) is located in the station of *śaraṇa*; it is endowed with the *śāntyatīta* kalā and is the instrument for perceiving sound.

The mental [organ] is the Great Liṅga, which takes its refuge in the station of Unity (aikyasthala); it is endowed with Śānti, Atīta, and Uttara, and is the means for grasping everything. In this manner, the sequential application of the Liṅga to the limbs of the organs of action is to be understood by yogins in their entirety, according to each respective Liṅga and its manifestation. Thus [ends verse 7].

In this context, although the locations of the sixfold liṅgas, such as the Mahāliṅga and others, are indeed the sixfold cakras beginning with the *brahmarandhra*— since they are perceptible precisely within those respective cakras—
nevertheless, even those liṅgas situated in the various cakras [are perceived] through the doors of their respective sense organs.

Because each sense organ has the nature of perceiving its respective object, they are designated by way of their specific marks (*liṅga*), and thus their nature as marks is described. This very sequence is found in the *Kenopaniṣad*, beginning with "Oṃ! By whom impelled does the mind fly forth, sent forth? and continuing with "the hearing of the hearing, the mind of the mind... [and so on].
Having described how the sense organs have as their respective objects the specific characteristics [of the self] through the passage beginning with "the mind," [the text continues]:
"That which is not expressed by speech, that by which speech is expressed—know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people here worship. And so forth.
This has been demonstrated by the prescription of objects for meditation in the form of those respective entities to be contemplated.
Furthermore, in the *Vātulottara*, it is stated that "here, the nose is called the mouth of the olfactory organ, which is the sign of conduct" (*ācāra-liṅga*), and so forth;
thus, the olfactory organs and the others are said to have the signs of conduct and the like as their mouths. However, [it does not mean that the senses themselves are the mouth].

The nature of being a *liṅga* (sign) is impossible for the senses, which are impermanent and insentient, because they cannot possess the essential nature of a sign that is permanent and sentient. Now, one might object:
even if they lack the essential nature of a sign, there is no inconsistency in describing them as the "locus of the sign" (*liṅgasthāna*).
If it is argued that their status as "faces of the *liṅga*"* (*liṅgamukhatva*) is also applicable [to these], we say no;

for the author has stated immediately thereafter that the sixfold wheels, beginning with the *ādhāra*, are themselves the locations of the sixfold *liṅgas*, beginning with the *ācāra*. Therefore, regarding the phrase "the nose of the nose" (*ghrāṇasya ghrāṇam*):

The meaning to be understood is that "the nose" refers to the olfactory sense-organ (ghrāṇendriya), which is the "mouth" of the Ācāraliṅga situated in the foundational wheel (ādhāracakra) and indicated by the term "nose. This is because even in the previously cited statement,
"the Ācāraliṅga is called the nose," it is used strictly as an indicative designation (upalakṣaṇavidhi).
The term "nose" (*ghrāṇa-pada*) is connected with the mark of conduct (*ācāra-liṅga*), but not as a qualifier. It should be noted that this very meaning is clarified in the *Kenopaniṣad*:
"The nose of the smelling [soul], which is the mark of conduct, is called the mouth; and likewise, the tongue of the tasting [soul] is called the tongue."
The face of the Guru-liṅga shall be the eye; likewise, the eye of the Śiva-liṅga shall be the face. The skin is said to be the face of the Liṅga whose form is the skin.
The ear is said to be the face of the Prasāda-liṅga, and the heart is [the face] of the heart itself.

The face of the Great Liṅga (Mahāliṅga) should be [placed] there; thus the face of the Liṅga is to be known as established in each respective limb. This has been explained in detail, but it is not written here for fear of prolixity. || 8 ||

Thus, the individual soul (jīva)— which, through its connection with the three states consisting of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, is delimited by the gross, subtle, and causal bodies, and takes the form of Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña—
is [purified] by its own guru through the threefold initiation (dīkṣā) in the three bodies.

Through the contemplation of the offering of each respective object to the sixfold liṅgas contained within the three joined liṅgas, one experiences the great bliss that consists in the unity with the *ghanaliṅga*. And so it is said:
"They eat what has been eaten by Rudra; they drink what has been drunk by Rudra; they smell what has been smelled by Rudra."

Therefore, according to the Vedic scripture beginning with "The Brāhmaṇas are those whose minds are perfectly tranquil," the devotee there, having taken the fragrant substance with his well-purified hand— the hand characterized by right conduct and endowed with the power of action— and while recollecting the *nakāra* mantra, offers it at the entrance of the sense of smell.

Having become an enjoyer of that grace, he becomes blissful. For the devotee of Maheśvara, having taken the substance of *rasa* with the hand of his refined intellect through unwavering devotion to the Guru-Liṅga who is endowed with the power of knowledge, and while recollecting the *makāra* mantra, offers it into the mouth of the organ of taste; thus becoming an enjoyer of that grace—

He becomes joyful. Indeed, one who partakes of the grace (*prasāda*) of the Śiva-liṅga— endowed with the power of will (*icchā-śakti*)— should, with vigilant devotion and a hand free from egoism, take hold of the physical object, recollect the *śikāra* mantra, offer it at the gateway of the sense of sight, and thus become an enjoyer of that grace.

He becomes blissful. The possessor of the *prāṇaliṅga*, however, having grasped the object of touch with his hand of flowers through the experience and devotion for the mobile *liṅga* conjoined with the primordial power (*ādiśakti*), while recollecting the *vākāra* mantra, offers it at the gateway of the sense of touch; thus becoming an enjoyer of its grace, he becomes blissful.

There is [this state]. But the *śaraṇa* [practitioner], having grasped the meaning of the word through the hand of good knowledge with blissful devotion toward the *liṅga* of grace belonging to the one endowed with supreme power (*parāśakti*), and while recollecting the mantra beginning with the letter *ya*, offers it into the opening of the sense of hearing; thus becoming an enjoyer of that grace, he becomes blissful. As for the *aikya* [practitioner]—

Having grasped the object of satisfaction with the hand of true being through the state of *samarasa* (equilibrium of flavors) toward the Great Liṅga endowed with the power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*),

and having offered it into the mouth of the mind while recollecting the *praṇava* mantra, one becomes blissful by partaking in that grace. Thus, for the individual soul who has made this offering, [dissolution occurs] in the Consciousness-Brahman.

O Goddess, because it is the place of rest, the syllable *oṃ* is the face; the two syllables *namaḥ* are the two arms; the syllable *śi* is the middle of the body; and the two syllables *vāya* are the two feet. The seat (*pīṭha*) is said to extend from the feet up to the knees;
that which reaches to the navel is the middle; and that which reaches to the heart is circular, extending up to the throat.
The cow-mouth (gomukha) is said to end at the midpoint between the eyebrows; the throat of the linga (liṅgakaṇṭha) is the head of the linga (liṅgamastaka).

Thus, from this statement, it is established that even each respective body possesses the nature of a *liṅga* by way of its mantric indicative power (*mantraliṅga*). Nevertheless, since worship is prescribed through the combination of ritual action (*kriyā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) for as long as one dwells in the body,
it should be understood that the practice of the identity of the *liṅga* and the limbs (*aṅgasāmarasya*) remains entirely unimpeded until the separation from the body.

Thus, because earth is a limb of devotion (*bhakti*), it becomes dissolved right there, since its nature is the support of consciousness (*ciddhṛti*). Because water is a limb of Maheśvara, those [waters] become dissolved right there, since their nature is the nourishment of consciousness (*cidāpyāyana*).
Because fire is a limb of grace (*prasāda*), that [fire] becomes dissolved right there, since its nature is the radiance of consciousness (*cidujvalana*).

Because wind has breath as its limb, it is dissolved right there, for its nature is vibration characterized by autonomy. Because space has the body as its limb, it is dissolved right there, for its nature is the pervasion of consciousness. [The object of knowledge...]

Because the mind, which consists of drops (*bindu*) distinguished by mental formations (*saṃskāra*), is a limb of oneness, it becomes dissolved right there, owing to its nature as consciousness-bliss (*cidānanda*). In this manner, because the conduct of the devotee is a limb of the *liṅga*, he becomes dissolved right there, due to his connection with the contemplation of the substance of fragrance. This applies to the Māheśvara.

Because it is an auxiliary of the *guruliṅga*, it becomes dissolved right there, due to its connection with the contemplation of the category of *rasa* (flavor). Because it is an auxiliary of the *prasādinaḥ śivaliṅga*, it becomes dissolved right there, due to its connection with the contemplation of the category of *rūpa* (form). [This applies to] the practitioner of the *prāṇaliṅga*.

Because it is a limb of the mobile liṅga, it becomes dissolved right there due to its connection with the contemplation of the object of touch. Because it is a limb of the liṅga of grace (prasāda) of the refuge, it becomes dissolved right there due to its connection with the contemplation of the object of sound. Of oneness...

Because it is a limb of the Great Liṅga (mahāliṅga), it becomes dissolved right there, due to its connection with the contemplation of all categories of existence. In this way, the Ācāra-liṅga becomes dissolved in the Guru-liṅga, because of its connection with the Iṣṭa-liṅga. The Guru-liṅga becomes dissolved in the Śiva-liṅga.

Because of its connection with the desired vital breath (*prāṇa*), the *śivaliṅga* becomes dissolved into the *jaṅgamaliṅga*, due to its connection with the *prāṇaliṅga*. The *jaṅgamaliṅga* becomes dissolved into the *prasādaliṅga*, due to its connection with the state of the vital breath (*prāṇabhāva*). The *prasādaliṅga* becomes dissolved into the *mahāliṅga*.
Because it is connected with the *bhāva-liṅga*, the *mahāliṅga* becomes merged in oneness with the *ghanaliṅga*,
owing to its nature as *saccidānanda*. Thus,
regarding the one hundred and one stages (*sthala*), beginning from the *piṇḍa* and ending with *jñānaśūnya*:

The sequence [of arguments] should also be investigated; since that has been explained in detail in our *Śivānubhavasiddhānta*, we shall desist here. Thus ends the *Śivādvaitaviveka*. [Thus ends the third chapter.]
[Now begins the fourth chapter.
Thus, in the manner previously described, the purification of the meaning of the great Mahāvākyas such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) is also established.
For instance, there is the subtle power consisting of both the conscious (cit) and the unconscious (acit), which is fit for the differentiation of name and form, and that which is qualified by it.
Consciousness distinguished by attributes such as omniscience,
pure consciousness distinguished by the subtle power consisting of the cit and acit which is incapable of being divided into name and form—
these three, perceived as one like a serpent and its coils, constitute the referent of the word *tat*.

It exists as the substratum of both consciousness and non-consciousness, characterized by the subtle powers of the distinct aspects of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and possessing attributes such as omniscience.

That pure consciousness which is qualified by a subtle power consisting of both conscious and unconscious elements, being incapable of differentiation between name and form (*nāmarūpa*), is the referent denoted by the word *tat*. Similarly, [pure consciousness] qualified by a gross power consisting of both conscious and unconscious elements, and characterized by attributes such as limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*) and so forth, [is the referent denoted by the word *tvam*].

Pure consciousness (śuddhacaitanya), characterized by a subtle power consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious— which is unfit for the differentiation of name and form— along with these three [name, form, and power], constitutes the denotative meaning of the term *tvaṃ* (you).

This is the substratum for both [the pure consciousness] and the consciousness characterized by the gross forms of the conscious and the unconscious, as well as by their powers and attributes such as limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*).

That pure consciousness which is denoted by the term *hūtam*— characterized by the subtle power of both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*), and which is incapable of being divided into name and form— that is the referent of the word *tvaṃ* (thou) in the great sentence "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), which [establishes the identity] of Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*) despite their being characterized by contradictory attributes.

Even though they lack the capacity to directly establish identity, they convey a single meaning through implication (*lakṣaṇā*) by means of three types of relationship. These three relationships consist of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words and the qualifier-qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*) relationship between their respective referents.

And there is the relationship of the indicated and the indicator between the inner self and its attributes. In that context, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two words, which have distinct grounds for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*). (The ground for application...)

The meaning is "the delimitor of capability" (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). It is the co-occurrence (*vṛtti*) of two words in a single referent. In the sentence "This is that Devadatta," the qualification by that time and that place is the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word "that" (*tat*); the qualification by this time and this place is the ground for the application of the word "this" (*idam*). And thus:

The relationship of *tātparya* (intended meaning) between these two words, which have distinct grounds for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*), resides in a single entity, Devadatta. Similarly, in the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) as well, the ground for the application of the word "That" (*tat*) is its qualification by the subtle powers of the conscious and unconscious (*cid-acit*).
The specific qualification by the power consisting of gross consciousness and non-consciousness is the ground for the application of the term *tvam* (thou). Thus,

although the two terms *tat* (that) and *tvam* have distinct grounds for their application, they both refer to a single reality qualified by the power consisting of subtle consciousness and non-consciousness, which is incapable of being divided into name and form.
The relation of purport (*tātparya-sambandha*) with pure consciousness is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). || 1 ||
The relationship between two entities is that of the qualifier and the qualified (the *vyāvartaka* being the qualifier—
that is, the distinguisher— and the *vyāvartya* being the qualified— that is, the object to be distinguished).
The state of these two is the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*), and that alone is the relation.

With the intention that [the relation] must be defined by both [terms], like a [mutual] connection, he states the relation of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva) along with an illustration, beginning with "And that":
namely, the relation of qualifier and qualified; and that [is found] in the case of "This is that Devadatta."

When it is realized that this body of Devadatta, qualified by this place, this time, and this word "this," which is denoted by the word "this," is not different from that body of Devadatta denoted by the word "that," which was qualified by that place and that time— then:

The referent of the word *tat* (that) is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) because it excludes difference residing in the referent denoted by the word *ayam* (this), while the referent of the word *ayam* is the qualified (*viśeṣya*) because it is that which is to be excluded.
Likewise, "he" (*saḥ*) refers to the body of Devadatta as denoted by the word *tat*, characterized by that [past] time and that [past] place.

When it is realized that this Devadatta-body, as qualified by this time and this place, is not different from that which is denoted by the word "this" (so'yam), then the referent of the word "this" functions as a qualifier by excluding difference residing in the referent of the word "that."

The state of being the qualified (viśeṣyatva) arises from the fact that something is to be excluded. Thus, in the manner of "This is that" and "That is this," there exists a mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified between the two referents by virtue of their excluding one another's differences. Similarly, here too, in the great sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), that which is "thou" (tvam)—

When it is realized that the consciousness qualified by the power consisting of gross *cit* and *acit*, which is denoted by the word "That" (*tat*), is not different from the consciousness qualified by the power consisting of subtle *cit* and *acit*, which is denoted by the word "Thou" (*tvam*), then the referent of the word "That" functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) by way of excluding the difference residing in the referent of the word "Thou."
Because the referent of the term *tvaṃ* (you) is that which is to be excluded [from the ultimate], it possesses the status of being the substantive (*viśeṣya*). Thus,

when it is realized that the consciousness qualified by the subtle power consisting of the sentient and insentient— which is denoted by the term *tat* (that)— is not different from the consciousness qualified by the gross power consisting of the sentient and insentient— which is denoted by the term *tvaṃ*— then...

The referent of the term *tvaṃ* (you) functions as a qualifier by excluding difference residing in the referent of the term *tat* (that), while the referent of the term *tat* functions as the qualificand because it is that which is to be excluded. Thus, in the Great Saying "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*), the two referents— the meanings of *tat* and *tvam*— serve to exclude each other's differences.
The relationship of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva) is to be understood. || 2 ||

The relationship between the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) and the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), however, is the relationship between the inner self (*pratyagātman*) and the attributes residing therein. A sentence that expresses the unique, defining attribute is a "defining statement" (*lakṣaṇavākya*); that which is to be expressed by it is the remaining [subject], the "object to be defined" (*lakṣya*). And thus, this is that...

In this sentence "Devadatta," there is [a connection] with the individual substance Devadatta as qualified by the property of being Devadatta— which is non-contradictory— after abandoning the contradiction between the two words or their respective meanings, namely, being qualified by that time and that place versus being qualified by this time and this place.
Just as there exists a relationship of the indicated and the indicator (*lakṣya-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*) between the word denoting Devadatta qualified by the state of being Devadatta [and Devadatta himself],

likewise, in the Great Sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), there occurs— by abandoning the qualification of the two words *tat* and *tvam*, or their respective referents, as being characterized by the powers of the subtle and gross forms of consciousness and non-consciousness which are mutually contradictory.

The relationship between the two words *tat* and *tvam* as the indicated (*lakṣya*) and the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) exists with respect to that consciousness which is qualified by its powers in the form of the subtle sentient and insentient, which are fit for the division of name and form that is not opposed to what is indicated by those two words.
(With the intention that there is "partial indication" (*bhāgalakṣaṇā*) in sentences such as "That thou art," he says: "This very [indication]... This very [indication] is called "partial indication.
Herein, there is indication of the two words *tat* and *tvam*, and of their respective referents, once their contradictory portions have been abandoned.
It should be understood that the indivisible consciousness of Paraśiva is the object of definition. || 3 ||

In that regard, indication (lakṣaṇā) is the operation [of a word] based on its inseparable connection with the denoted meaning [when the primary meaning is not accepted due to contradiction with another means of knowledge]. Indication is held to be the operation [of a word] toward that which is inseparably connected with the primary meaning.
Thus, the sense is that *lakṣaṇā* (indication) consists precisely in the connection with a possible meaning. And that [indication] is threefold:
*jahallakṣaṇā*, *ajahallakṣaṇā*, and *jahadajahallakṣaṇā*.
*Jahallakṣaṇā* is the function [of a word] toward another meaning related to it, having completely abandoned its own expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*).
And this [metaphorical application] is not appropriate here in the same way as it is in the sentence "the cowherd settlement is on the Gaṅgā," because in that case the sentence-meaning—
characterized by the relationship of locus and located between the Gaṅgā and the cowherd settlement—
is entirely contradictory; therefore, having completely abandoned that sentence-meaning, one resorts to another meaning related to it, namely the bank (*tīra*).

Since [indication] is appropriate, *jahallakṣaṇā* (indication involving the abandonment of the primary meaning) is consistent. However, in this case, because there is a contradiction regarding only a portion of the sentence-meaning— which consists in the unity of consciousness qualified by the power (*śakti*) that has the form of the subtle and gross phenomenal world (*prapañca*)— one must abandon even the other portion [of the primary meaning] through another type of indication.
Because it would be illogical, the "exclusive" (jahat) indication is not tenable. || 4 ||

Indication that does not abandon the literal meaning (*ajahallakṣaṇā*) is the cessation of the literal sense in favor of something related to it. However, this [type of indication] is not applicable here, as in the sentence "The red one runs" (*śoṇo dhāvati*). For in that case, because the literal meaning of the sentence—characterized by the movement of the quality red—is contradictory [to the fact of running], [the quality] is not abandoned [in favor of the substance].

In that case, since it is possible to avoid contradiction by means of a definition characterized by the horse and so forth which serve as its substratum, *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-abandoning indication) is appropriate. But here,
[the object] is characterized by the oneness of consciousness qualified by the power (*śakti*) appearing in the forms of the subtle and gross phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

Because the meaning of the sentence is contradictory, even if some meaning related to it were indicated (*lakṣita*) without abandoning that [contradictory] sense, it would be impossible to resolve that contradiction; therefore, *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-abandoning indication) is not tenable.
Consequently, the comprehension of the meaning of the Great Sentence occurs only through *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (partial abandonment-indication). Thus it has been said:
By the venerable teacher [in the *Śivādvaitasudhākara*]: "Because of their identity as one essence, the *jahatī* [type of indication] is not possible;

likewise, the *ajahat-lakṣaṇā* is impossible due to contradiction. Therefore, like the two referents 'he' and 'this,' the *bhāga-lakṣaṇā* would be appropriate for the words *tat* and *tvam* without fault"—thus it is said regarding the comprehension of the meaning of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*).
Only the *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (the indicative function that both excludes and includes) has been accepted.

In that context, *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (the indicative function where part [of the primary meaning] is abandoned) consists in the operation of the word upon one part [of its primary meaning] by abandoning another part; and this occurs,

for example, in the sentence "This is that Devadatta" or in its referent, because there is a contradiction regarding a portion of the sentence-meaning characterized as Devadatta qualified by both that time and this time.
Setting aside the contradictory portions characterized by "that time" and "this time," it indicates only the non-contradictory portion that is Devadatta; likewise,
so does the sentence "That thou art" (tattvamasi) or its meaning.

Because there is a contradiction regarding the meaning of the sentence in the aspect that [Brahman] is a single consciousness qualified by powers having the forms of both subtle and gross manifestation, one must discard the contradictory aspects of subtlety and grossness; [what remains is] that which is qualified by powers consisting of the subtle sentient and insentient, which are not subject to the division of name and form.

It characterizes pure consciousness alone; thus it has been said: "The signified (liṅga) is expressed by the word *tat*, while the body (aṅga) is declared by the word *tvam*. This relationship of identity between these two is expressed by the word *asi*.
For whomsoever this contemplation of the sentence shines continuously, [he attains liberation].

Through the instruction of the Guru, he is said to possess the connection between the *liṅga* and the *aṅga*. Thus, he in whom the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of this connection between the *liṅga* and the *aṅga* exists—he is a yogi, he is omniscient, and he is called one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). Then, having abandoned the referential meanings denoted by the words *liṅga* and *aṅga* through right intellect, [he attains the state of non-duality].
Having identified that indicated object, one should contemplate, "I am indeed That.

Merely by the birth of right knowledge arising from the connection between the sign (liṅga), the body (aṅga), and the words, [the world]—along with its companion, ignorance—has not been, does not exist, and will not exist. Thus [ends the verse]. 6.

Furthermore, this sentence "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) is not intended as a mere eulogy, like the statement "Thou art Indra," because that would entail the redundancy of its ninefold repetition. Indeed, a eulogy is never repeated in this manner following repeated challenges. For this very reason, it is not an explanatory passage (arthavāda), since it is not subordinate to anything else.

For in this context, no other principal statement is found that could serve as the basis for this [passage] being an explanatory supplement (arthavāda). Nor is it figurative, as in the case of "this is the king's man" where one says "this is the king," because it is impossible for identity to be figurative when the two things are not cognized as distinct. Nor is there a reversal [of the relationship].
Or rather, doubt may arise here because of the self-evident validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) of scripture.

Therefore, the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) and others have as their ultimate purport an indivisible reality (*akhaṇḍārtha*), because, while having as their purport merely a substance that is neither cause nor effect, they are sentences of grammatical coordination (*samānādhikaraṇa-vākya*).

It is like the sentence, "This is that Devadatta. Thus, since the two words are restricted to an indivisible (akhaṇḍa) meaning, their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not possible without *lakṣaṇā* (indication), because there is a contradiction regarding the literal meanings of the words. And so it has been said concerning the referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam*:

"The cognition that [Śiva] is that which is non-contradictory—the indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha) consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss—having abandoned the mutually contradictory denoted meanings (vācyārtha) produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), such as the forms of the linga and the body;
that [cognition] is called 'relationship' (sambandha) by those who know the Vedāntas and Āgamas. Thus [ends verse 7].

Having explained in detail the meaning of the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), which establishes the consciousness of Paraśiva—also known as Ghanaliṅga—I shall now describe the meaning of the experiential statement from the Yajurveda:
"I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*). Regarding this "I am Brahman," [it is related to] the previously mentioned "That thou art."

The individual soul (*jīva*), characterized by the power (*śakti*) of the gross forms of consciousness and non-consciousness as grasped by the term *tat-pada* within the Great Saying (*mahāvākya*), is denoted by the word *ahaṃ* (I). Likewise, the Supreme Śiva (*paraśiva*), characterized by the power of the subtle forms of consciousness and non-consciousness as grasped by the term *tat-pada*, is denoted by the word *brahma*.
Thus, what was expressed by the word *asi* (you are) regarding their identity is here expressed by the word *asmi* (I am).

And so, the very meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), which was previously understood through indirect knowledge, is now experienced directly through the indivisible sentence "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*). [This occurs] from the mouth of the venerable Guru nine times, beginning with "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).

Upon hearing these words, after the realization of oneness with the pure Paraśiva has arisen for a certain qualified seeker regarding the inner Self— which is distinct from all visible objects, beginning with the body and ending with the ego-sense, which are all inert— [he] finds his opportunity.

The meaning is that one who desires to know, through direct experience, that which is liberated from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and consists of the single essence of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), recollecting the meaning of the great statement (*mahāvākya*) "I am Brahman" as taught by the teacher, experiences the bliss of one's own Self in the form of the identity between the dense *liṅga* and the individual soul. Thus it has been said:

Mahādeva, whose nature is the *liṅga*, is characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*). Indeed, the individual soul (*jīvātman*), constrained by worldly existence, is of the nature of the *aṅga*. Therefore, Sadāśiva in the form of the *liṅga* is designated as "that state" (*tatpada*) by the wise.

Indeed, by the word "thou" (tvaṃ), the individual soul (jīva), characterized by transmigratory existence, is denoted as the body; that which is the referent of "thou" as the essential nature of the body is indeed the referent of the word "I" (ahaṃ). The Supreme Lord, whose nature is consciousness, is the indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha) of both the words "thou" and "I. This is because the objects denoted by the words "thou" and "I"—namely the body and so forth—possess neither the meaning of the suffix "tat" (that-ness) nor the meaning of the suffix "tvat" (thou-ness).

"Because they are always contradictory, the referent indicated by the words 'Thou' and 'I'—the individual soul (jīvātman)—is of the nature of a limb; if it were inauspicious, then [the Self], which is eternal bliss, would not perceive it at all. In reality, taking up the referent indicated by these words, the Great Saying "That Thou Art" brings about the very state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*) between the signified object (*liṅga*) and the limb (*aṅga*), as understood through indirect cognition.
Through the indivisible statement "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*), by means of the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*), one experiences [Brahman] directly;
through the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) that "I am Śiva, whose nature is supreme bliss," one becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). As it has been said:
"He in whom such a contemplation of the connection between the Linga and the body exists—he is a yogi, and he is omniscient."
He is called one liberated while living. Thus [ends the verse]. 8.

In this regard, although the words such as "I" (aham) function with respect to the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) through their own respective modes of operation— namely, by means of the grounds for application (pravṛttinimitta) and the limiting adjuncts (upādhi)— nevertheless,

those two [grounds and adjuncts] relate to Him by way of being the connection between the individual self (svātman) and Śiva, which serves as the mediating link in the indirect relationship (paraṃparāsambandha).

Furthermore, the relationship of the governed and the governor between one's own self and Śiva is indeed understood from words such as "I" (aham) and others, which extend up to the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin).

Therefore, since the primary denotative power (śakti) of words like "I" exists in the Supreme Śiva as the Inner Controller when they are employed by those who have surrendered (prapanna), [the usage is justified].

Since there is no sublation [of this experience], metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is improper. [This is because] Paraśiva exists as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of the individual souls (*jīva*), and the souls exist as His bodies; thus, [the notions] "I am a human," "I am a god," "I am fair-skinned," and "I am stout" [are directly perceived].

If, as in such cases, the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of words such as "I" and so forth is established in the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), and thus the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman alone is perceived, then for what purpose is this non-difference established by abandoning the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*) and adopting the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*)? And for what purpose [is it said] that the individual soul and Brahman [are identical] in their essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*)?
