Anticipating the objection that "even so, two powers consisting of the gross and the subtle— the conscious and the unconscious— are accepted in order to establish their distinction," he refutes it with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).
And thus, [it refers to] the Supreme Śiva, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, who possesses all powers, and who is omniscient.
The entire universe, consisting of both sentient and insentient beings, becomes the object of identification through the state of identity [with Him];

thus, Paraśiva is said to be the self of all. As for individual souls (*jīvas*), who are of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), their respective bodies alone consist of the gross form of the power (*śakti*) of both consciousness and matter (*cid-acit*).

Because they have become objects of the conceit of identity [with Him], individual souls (jīvas) are said to possess distinct, separate bodies as their very selves. Since Paraśiva is the possessor of all conceits and is endowed with all powers, He is able to act upon the entire universe exactly as He wills.

And so it is said in the Gītā: "With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, with ears everywhere in the world, the Lord stands encompassing all. O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion (māyā), as if they were mounted on a machine."

Thus, because individual souls (jīvas) possess self-identification with their respective bodies and are characterized by limited power, they have the capacity—provided there is no obstruction—to move only their own respective bodies through their own will and effort. Therefore, all of this is produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi); [one should understand it] by setting aside those adjuncts.

This description of the meaning of the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*), undertaken by first discarding the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*) and adopting the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*), is solely for the sake of easy understanding by disciples that one's own true nature (*nijasvarūpa*) is indeed the very nature of Supreme Śiva, which is pure consciousness (*śuddhacaitanya*). In this established doctrine (*siddhānta*), regarding the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*):

It should be understood that this is not the falsity (mithyātva) stated in the Advaita doctrine, but rather the impermanence consisting in the state of abiding as the nature of the cause for that which has entered the state of being an effect. Nevertheless,
everything consisting of the powers (śakti) whose nature is both conscious (cit) and unconscious (acit), exists through identity (tādātmya) with Paraśiva, who is the self of all.

The object of the world-ego is [the Lord]; however, for individual souls (jīvas), whose nature is consciousness, the object of their ego is merely their respective bodies, which consist of the gross form of the power of both consciousness and the non-conscious. Thus, having first abandoned those respective limiting adjuncts (upādhis) that have become the objects of their ego, one should take up the intended meaning (lakṣyārtha).
It should be understood that the comprehension of the meaning of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) is intended solely for the easy understanding of disciples. || 9 ||

In the passage "Brahman is consciousness" (*aitareyopaniṣad* 3.3), by the term "consciousness," [it is meant] through each respective sense organ, as described in *aitareyopaniṣad* 3.1: "by which one sees, by which one hears,
by which one smells odors," and so forth.
Having described its nature as consisting of the sixfold marks (*ṣaḍvidhaliṅga*) which contemplate their respective objects—

as stated in the *Aitareya Upaniṣad* (3.2) starting from "This heart... and ending with "...all these are names of consciousness"— it is shown to be the collective totality (*samaṣṭirūpa*) of the sixfold marks.
The *bhāvaliṅga* has been established by the word "Brahman" [in the Aitareya Upaniṣad 3.3],

beginning with "This is Brahman, this is Indra," and ending with "All this is guided by wisdom (*prajñā*), established in wisdom," which demonstrates that the entire world, consisting of both sentient and insentient beings, has that [Brahman] as its nature.

Having further established that wisdom (*prajñā*) is the foundation, he has described by the phrase "the foundation is wisdom" the power of wisdom (*prajñā-śakti*)— which is the unique attribute constituting the culmination [of all things] and whose essential nature consists of the subtle *cit* (consciousness) and *acit* (non-consciousness); and then, by the phrase "Brahman is consciousness" (*prajñānaṃ brahma*), he [describes] the principle of Supreme Śiva.
This has been established. As it is said in the *Śivādvaitasudhākara*:

"That by which [the Self], through the medium of the senses, hears and articulates this, sees and tastes, and likewise smells this by its very nature—that is the Supreme, known as the Bhāvaliṅga, [perceived] through wisdom."

It has been proclaimed: "That which is the single consciousness within Viṣṇu and the other principal deities, as well as among humans, animals, and birds—that is Brahman; that Liṅga consists of consciousness and bliss.
Therefore, the understanding of the meaning of the statement is that the Supreme Brahman, consisting of the six stages (ṣaṭsthala), is indeed the Bhāvaliṅga. || 10 ||

In the passage "This Self is Brahman" (*Māṇḍūkyopaniṣad* 3), by the two words "this" (*ayam*) and "Self" (*ātman*), there is the rejection of that which is denoted by the word "this"— pointed out with the finger— and which is conditioned by the three states consisting of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, and is delimited by the gross, subtle, and causal bodies, and associated with the limbs of renunciation and the limbs of enjoyment.
The individual soul (jīva) is called by another name, "Brahman. By the term "Brahman" is meant that which is devoid of the three states,
has attained the fourth state (turiya), is not delimited by the three bodies, and is the collective totality of the forms of the *iṣṭaliṅga*, *prāṇaliṅga*, and *bhāvaliṅga*.

The supreme reality of Śiva is said to consist of the *ghanaliṅga*. Thus, in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, beginning with "Oṃ—this syllable is this [all]" (MāU 3), and ending with "This Self is Brahman; this very Self is fourfold," [the text] describes it by way of the form of the primordial *praṇava*.

Having first demonstrated in a general manner—by means of establishing the nature of Brahman—that the individual self (jīvātman), as qualified by the word "this" (ayam), is included within the fourfold forms residing in Brahman; he then demonstrates that very same point again, beginning with the passage:
"He whose sphere is the waking state, who is conscious of the external world... [he is] the enjoyer of bliss, whose face is the mind."

Having described the threefold nature [of the Self] as being delimited by the three bodies based on the three states of waking and so forth, up to the words "the wise one is the third foot," [the text] begins with "He is the Lord of all,
He is the All-knowing," and continues until "the cessation of the phenomenal world, the peaceful, the auspicious, the non-dual."

By the conclusion of the passage, "They consider him the fourth; he is the Self; he is to be known," it is established that his essential nature is that of the Supreme Śiva-tattva, which consists of the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*) in the form of the dense *liṅga* (*ghanaliṅga*), unconditioned by the three bodies (*trikāya*) attained in the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*). This was stated by the venerable Ciddhanaguru (this is the meaning).

By the venerable teacher (*gurucaraṇa*) [in the *Śivādvaitasudhākara*]: "Because of its connection with the three bodies, the individual soul (*jīvātman*), which is associated with the three states (*avasthā*) and denoted by the word 'body' (*aṅga*), is called 'this Self' (*ayam ātmā*).
But Śiva, who is directly devoid of bodies and free from the three states, is the Fourth (*turīya*) and is indeed denoted by the word 'sign' (*liṅga*)."
It is called Brahman. Therefore, by way of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), the individual soul (jīva) is none other than Śiva; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus ascertained with the mind, one should contemplate "I am Śiva. Through the realization of the identity of Śiva and the individual soul, one shall attain supreme bliss. Thus it is said.

Therefore, [it is established] that in the triad of Śiva, Śakti, and Jīva— which, being distinguished by the eight enclosures (aṣṭāvaraṇa) and the five conducts (pañcācāra) well-known from all the Śrutis, Āgamas, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas, reveals the secret of the essential identity (sāmarasya) between the Liṅga and the Aṅga consisting of the reflective awareness of the full "I" (pūrṇāhaṃvimarśana) which is non-different from the entire universe— [the aforementioned principles reside].

It is precisely within the Śivādvaita Siddhānta—the repository of the essential harmony of the three categories; the expounder of the four pillars of knowledge, action, yoga, and conduct; the quintessence of all the twenty-eight divine Āgamas beginning with the *Kāmika* and ending with the *Vātula*; and the synonym for the non-dualism qualified by Śakti—that the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*) find their true meaning.
Thus, everything is consistent through the principle of samanvaya (harmonious coordination). This concludes the "Discernment of the Meaning of the Great Sayings" (Mahāvākyārthaviveka).
[This is the Fourth Chapter.]
[For those whose minds are intent on devotion to Śiva, conduct befitting Śiva, and the worship of Śiva...]
This mirror has been fashioned by me for the purpose of realizing one's own true nature. || 1 ||

[Thus ends the work] of the venerable Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya Bhagavatpāda, the sovereign lord of the preeminent city of Puvvallī, who was a supreme master among the wandering mendicants of the Paramahaṃsa order, independent in all philosophical systems, one who had reached the further shore of the ocean of words, logic, and epistemology, and an incarnation of the Supreme Śiva.

The milk of the illustrious Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita-siddhānta, produced from the lotus-hand of the venerable Śivācārya— a treasury of consciousness— who occupies the throne of the *Śrīśivādvaitabhāṣya* established by the great monastery of Pūvallī Pañcavarṇa.
The *Śivādvaitadarpaṇa*, composed by Śivānubhava Śivācārya— who possesses the splendor of the moon that illuminates both shores—
is complete. May all be offered unto Śiva.
